Q.10(a) The New Millennium Indian Technology Leadership Initiative Programme was initiated in the year 2000-2001 with the objective
 of a global leadership in technology with a allocation of Rs. 50 crores. At the R.E. stage the allocation was surprisingly reduced to half of
 the total amount -i.e. Rs. 25 crores. Whether the sharp reduction in the allocation at R.E. stage indicates that the Department could not
 fulfill its objectives in the last year; if so, what are the reasons?
(b)             Interestingly in the year 2001-2002, the B.E. has been again hiked to Rs. crores. Please explain the reasons for the same?
Ans. (a) A special grant of Rs. 50.00 crore was approved for the new scheme New Millennium Indian Technology Leadership Initiative
 (NMITLI) during the year 2000-01. The scheme is to provide support to innovation centered scientific & technological developments as
 a vehicle to attain for the country a global leadership position, at least in some selected niche areas in a true 'Team India' effort. The
 operationalisation of the scheme required not only innovative thinking to identify the select areas but also national consultations and
 involvement. Thus wide ranging and widespread national consultations were organized. Over 1000 personal letters were addressed by
 DG, CSIR to leaders in academia, S&T, industry etc. seeking suggestions for these niche areas. A special  meeting  of  the  CSIR 
 Advisory  Board (AB)  was held to discuss the NMITLI scheme.
Based on the directions of AB, national and regional level Workshops were organized on the occasion of National Technology bay by all CSIR
 laboratories. A special advertisement was inserted in leading national dailies again on National Technology Day and over 8500 NMITLI posters,
 seeking suggestions on potential niche areas, were sent to diverse educational and R&D establishments. Thus the process of national consultations
 involved fountainheads of wisdom from diverse walks of life. This generated overwhelming enthusiasm in the S&T and industry. community and
 suggestions for over 1000 ideas were received. Thereafter a very stringent and rigorous system of screening, expert evaluation and assessment,
 championing and brainstorming was set up. In this, eminent experts from Industry and Academia and Research Institutions were associated; over
 4000 high quality man days were devoted to identifying 28 potential niche opportunity areas from over 1000 bare ideas and another 2000
 specialists man days were devoted formulating strategic technology projects. In the first phase 12 niche ideas were considered and only nine of
 these ideas were projectised with the help of internationally recognized experts from R&D and industry.    These detailed projects were then
 subjected to techno- economic evaluation by a High-Powered Committee (HPC) and the recommendations of the HPC were subsequently
 considered by the Governing Body of CSIR and nine projects at a total cost of about Rs. 54 crore spread over a period of 2-3 years were approved
 with the first years outlay of around Rs.35 crore. Thus a great amount of national churning went into devising a transparent system of
 implementation and national consultation in perfecting the niche opportunity technology areas into project mode. Thus, the surrender of Rs.25
 crore at the RE stage was a prudent step to optimize on investments and come up with winnable projects.
(b)    In addition to these nine projects taken up in the first phase,  remaining sixteen niche technology areas are being projectised on the
 same stringent     and     rigorous      basis  as evolved. Thus the Rs. 50 crore allocation sought for 2061-2002 is to partly meet the
 allocations for the second year for the nine projects and the first year installment for the new projects that would be taken up. Thus the
 full allocation of Rs. 50 crore is expected to be utilized during 2001-2002.
Qll.   It has been mentioned that the DSIR support for the Programme Aimed at Technological Self Reliance (PASTER) is catalytic and
 major part of the financial support to any project under the Programme has been from the industry.
(a)        The Committee would like to know the details of share between DSIR and the industry under the programme, besides furnishing
 details of different projects supported by the industry.
(b)      With an enhanced allocation of Rs.  8.40 crores in the current year as compared to Rs. 7.20 crores both at B.E. & R.E. of 2000-01,
 what projects Department purposes to undertake in the year under review?
Ans.(a) The   PATSER   Scheme   provides   partial funding   through Grants-in-aid to industry for projects taken up in association with
 other research organizations/ institutions for Development and demonstration of new/improved products and processes, as well as
 absorption & up-gradation of imported technology. DSIR's support cover inter-alia, part of the costs of prototype, pilot, plant,
 consultancy, test equipment/test rigs, testing & trials, etc. Generally, DSIIR support is 30- 40% of the total project cost and the remaining
 expenditure is met by the Industry. Till now, DSIR has supported over 110 projects envisaging a total project cost of Rs. 158 crores with
 DSIR's share being Rs. 47 crores i.e. around 30% on an average.
 
 (b)    Some of the products/processes developed under PATSER include: Digested organic supplement from agricultural waste, Earth
 moving machinery such as 70T dumper, 200 HP front-end loader, IOT excavator, 460 HP Wheel dozer; Xenon and Crypton lamps for
 Laser pumping, 6 Hi cold rolling mill, fresh Detonating Cards for shaped charges.
In 2000-01, 75 projects are in progress such as L(+) Tartaric Acid from Tamarind, a mechanized process for utilization of distillery
 effluents for production of biocomposts, Heat resistant slurry explosives, 500 KW Gas Turbine for co-generation in process plants. High
 Speed Machining Centre, Computerized Braille Printing system and Material handling stockers, tow tractors, etc.
During 2001-02 around 25 new projects and around 85 on-going projects for technology development and demonstration are
 planned to be supported. Besides inviting fresh proposals from industry, DSIR will proactively interact with other ministries for
 identification of new products/processes required and promote technology development projects with small and medium enterprises.
 Besides supporting the projects, DSIR will organize/ support more interactions of industry, research organizations and concerned
 agencies for identifying future trends and needs for new/improved technologies.

Q13.   To what extent the budgetary support remained unutilized during the year 2000-2001 and what are the reasons therefor?
Ans.  The Revised estimates for 2000-01 for CSIR was reduced by Rs. 59.77 crore, this constituted Plan reduction of Rs. 27.52 crore and
 Non-Plan of Rs. 32.25 crore. This was due to a surrender of Rs. 25 crore under Plan for the new scheme New Millennium Indian
 Technology Leadership Initiatives (NMITLI) as explained in the question no. 10. The remaining Rs. 34.77 crore was reduced as an
 economic measures. In respect of OSIR, a total of Rs.9.26 crore is the surrender from the B.E. for the year 2000-2001. This includes
 Rs.3.76 crore under Revenue and Rs.5.50 crore under Capital. At the RE stage, the budgetary support was cut by Rs.2.63 crore. A further
 saving of Rs.6.63 crore is anticipated under various schemes due to inadequate number of desired   project  proposals  and  non-
fulfillment of necessary conditions/requirements by the beneficiaries for release of funds.
Q.14  A mention has been made in the Notes on Demands for Grants 2001-2002 about the Residential Buildings, staff quarters and other
 amenities. This is an important area with regard to the welfare of the officers and staff of the Ministry/DSIR including CSIR and
 Laboratories. What are the details of the project, including cost and the member of quarters/details of amenities sought to be provided
 and the percentage of satisfaction enjoyed by the staff in this regard?
Ans.  CSIR is grateful to the Committee for its sustained support to improve the housing and other amenities for the employees. This is
 the 'psychic' satisfaction that helps to attract and retain some talent in CSIR. The location of laboratories is divided under 3 categories
 viz. those in (i) Metro cities (ii) other towns and (iii) remote areas. The present level of satisfaction and the targets set for satisfaction for
 the three categories are metros: 13% vs 50%; other towns: 46% vs. 70% and remote areas; 57% vs. 80%. Thus there is substantial
 unsatiated demand. The major activity in 2000-2001 is improving the housing satisfaction level at the metros at Bangalore, Hyderabad &
 Delhi where inroads of IT sector on HR awe being felt and in remote areas like Palampur and Karaikudi where appropriate talent needs
 to be attracted and retained. In 2001-2002 the initiatives of 2000-2001 will be completed and activities in 'other towns' like,
 Bhubneshwar, Dhanbad, Mysore & Nagpur, will be initiated.

 R E P O R T
 
1.   The setting up of a separate Department of Biotechnology (DBT) under the Ministry of Science and Technology in 1986 gave a new impetus to
 the development of the field of modern biology and biotechnology in India.  In more than a decade of its existence, the Department has promoted
 and accelerated the pace of development of biotechnology in the country.  The Department has made significant achievements in the growth and
 application of biotechnology in the broad areas of agriculture, health care, animal sciences, environmental and industry.
      More than a decade of concerted effort in research and development in identified areas of modern biology and biotechnology have given rich
 dividends.  The proven technologies at the laboratory level have been scaled up and demonstrated in field.  Patenting of innovations, technology
 transfer to industries and close interaction with them have given a new direction to biotechnology research.  Initiatives have been taken to promote
 transgenic research in plants with emphasis on pest and disease resistance, nutritional quality, silk-worm genome analysis, molecular biology of
 human genetic disorders, brain research, plant genome research, development, validation and commercialization of diagnostic kits and vaccines
 for communicable diseases, food biotechnology, biodiversity conservation and bioprospecting, setting up of micro propagation parks and
 biotechnology based development for SC/ST, rural areas, women and for different States.  Department of Biotechnology (DBT) has been
 interacting with more than 5,000 scientists per year in order to utilize the existing expertise of the universities and other national laboratories. 
 There has been close interaction with the State Governments particularly through State S&T Councils for developing biotechnology application
 projects, demonstration of proven technologies, and training of human resource in a number of States and Union Territories.  The impact of the
 biotechnology related developments in agriculture, health care, environment and industry, has already been visible and the efforts are now
 culminating into products and processes.  More than 5000 research publications, 4000 post-doctoral students, several technologies transferred to
 industries and patents filed including US patents, can be considered as a modest beginning.  A unique feature of the department has been the deep
 involvement of the scientific community of the country through a number of technical task forces, advisory committees and individual experts in
 identification, formulation, implementation and monitoring of various programmes and activities.  Necessary guidelines of transgenic plants,
 recombinant vaccines and drugs have also been evolved.  A strong base of indigenous capabilities has been created.  The field of biotechnology
 both for new innovations and applications would form a major research and commercial endeavour for socio-economic development in the next
 millennium.
2.   The main responsibilities of this Department are:
(i)
        To evolve integrated plans and programmes in Biotechnology;
(ii)   Identify specific programmes of Research and Development and oversee related research and manufacturing activities for biologicals;
(iii)  Identify, set up and support centres of excellence for research and development in biotechnology and ensure proper dovetailing of these
 activities with national priorities;
(iv)
     Act as a screening, advising and approving body of Government with regard to import and transfer of new technologies for the
 manufacture of biologicals and biotechnological products and their intermediates;
 
(v)
      Evolve safety guidelines for biotechnology research, development and manufacturing in India;
(vi)     To act as the Central agency for the import of genetically manipulated materials, culture cells, specimens, tissue and biotech products
 including DNA and RNA of any type and for promoting their production in the country;
(vii) Serve as the interministerial and interagency nodal point for all specific international, bilateral and multilateral research and development
 collaboration in the area of biotechnology and act as the nodal point for all technology transfers in the area of biotechnology;
(viii) Manufacture and application cell-based vaccines;
(ix)     To evolve programmes of human resource development in the area of biotechnology;
(x)      To act as the administrative Department for autonomous institutions and ICGEB;
(xi)     Serve as the authorised Department of Government in respect of legislative Parliamentary
      requirements in all areas mentioned under Allocation of Business for the Department.
3.      Biotechnology as a branch of modern biology is hardly two decades old and it is the fastest growing branch of modern science.   It is rapidly
 becoming the cornerstone of industrial development and leading us to the brink of bio-industrial revolution.  In fact, we are now in biotech century
 and our way of life is likely to be more fundamentally transformed in the decades to come. The present day definition of biotechnology is the
 application of scientific and engineering principles to the processing materials by biological agents to produce goods and services.  The
 applications of biotechnology are so wide that virtually every industry including pharmaceuticals, textiles, aquaculture, chemicals, household
 products, manufacturing, environmental cleaning, food processing and forensics, are using the technology. 
4.      Biotechnology is emerging as a major player for enhancing the food productivity, nutritional status, sustainable utilization of biological
 resources, prospecting of new molecules and genes, identification and characterization of biological wealth, development of new vaccines,
 diagnostics and drugs, pollution abatement through biotechnological route, waste recycling, etc.  Bioinformatics and human resource development
 have given rich dividends in terms of highly skilled trained human resource available in the country and a strong information network being
 utilized by a large number of scientists.
5.   The Committee was informed that the Department transferred a number of technologies of diagnostics, tissue cultured plants and biofertilizers
 and biopesticides to the industry, had established more bioinformatic centres and new teaching programmes:  Special initiative was taken by the
 Department to organise a Brain Storming Session on the post Human Genome Sequencing and plan a future strategy.  Emphasis was also laid on

 generate biotechnology activities of relevance in their respective states.  DBT has been closely associated with their development and planning

6.   The   Committee has also been informed that the autonomous institutions have done very well in producing of excellent quality publications
 and generation of new products and technologies.  The research publications from all the autonomous institutions have high citation index and
 impact factor.  The peer reviewing and the monitoring mechanisms have been further strengthened and streamlined.  Necessary economy

BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
7.   Based on the recommendation of the working group, the Ninth Plan proposal was submitted to Planning Commission. The outlay of Rs.1026
 crores for period of five years (1997-2002) was proposed against which an outlay of Rs 675 crores has been recommended. Financial summary of

The allocation of Rs.186.34 crores allocated for the year 2001-2002 includes 175.00 crores for plan and Rs.11.34 crores for non-plan activities (Annexure I). The increase amounting
 to Rs.35.00 crores over BE of Rs.125.00 crores (plan) of the year 2000-2001 is mainly in the plan budget.  2001-2002,  being the last year of the 9 th plan, most of the projects were
 being undertaken within the scope of ongoing schemes/programmes.
8.   While the Department would continue to pursue the R&D leads towards product and process development, initiate major programmes in
 genomics and related areas, strengthen technology transfer mechanisms for rapid commercialization of technologies developed for societal and
 economic benefit of the country on an environmentally sound basis, some new initiatives in the area of human genetics and genome analysis as
 per the recommendations of the brain storming workshop on post genome perspectives are proposed to be considered during the year.  Besides,
 several projects of socio-economic relevance based on the needs of the country have been initiated.
9.   Many major activities initiated during the current 9 th plan would provide such dividends by the end of the plan period by promoting by  the end of the plan period by promoting
 foreign direct investment and products and processes in the field of health, care agriculture and industry  for the
benefit of society.  Indian Industries are expected to come forward to set up Biotech ventures.  Basic research on all aspects of biotechnology would be perused.   The allocation (Plan)
 for the Department of Biotechnology has gone up to Rs.175 crores for the financial year 2001-2002 as  against Rs.140 crores at R.E. stage and Rs.125 crores at B.E. stage in 2000-
01.  Asked whether the increase in allocation was necessitated by the erosion in the value of money or due to inclusion of new  items of work, the Committee was informed that the
 Department planned to initiate establishment of “GEN-NET INDIA” to cure, control and care genetic  disorders prevalent in the country along with the development of network
 programmes on human genome diversity and biochips in genomoics towards gene identification /diagnostics. Comparative genomics, data annotation, proteomics, pharmaco genomics
 and work on some microbial genomics would be started. Besides an Integrated approach towards utilisation and conservation of medicinal plants for herbal drug development employing
 biotechnology tools and techniques would be started. The Department also shall continue its recently started Indian initiatives on Rice Genome Sequencing and activities of National
 Bioresource Development Board. 
10.  The Committee observes that it is not opposed to enhanced allocations to the Department.  While it is necessary that the Department
 keeps itself posted with the developments abroad in the field of biotechnology, it should choose projects with utmost caution with a view
 to ensure that they are in the best interests of the country. 
AGRICULTURAL BIOTECHNOLOGY    
11.  During 2000-01 the Department received 400 R&D projects out of which 100 projects have been sanctioned in various disciplines, which
 include, among other Basic Research in Modern Biology, Agricultural Biotechnology, Biological Control of Plant Pests, Diseases and weeds,
 Biofertilizers, Biodiversity Conservation and  Environment, Medical Biotechnology, Human Genetics and Genome Analysis.
12.  The Department has continued its efforts to enhance food and agriculture production, quality and nutritional improvement, prevention of pre-
and post harvest losses and to ensure environmental sustainability. The Department carries research in three types of activities; R&D projects in
 priority crops; multi-institutional project on development of transgenics and quality trait studies.  Department also supports identified plant
 molecular biology programmes and its mandate relates to problems of priority crops, development of transgenics, quality improvement and basic
 research in the area of plant molecular biology. It also achieved success in basic plant biotechnology and plant genome research.
13.      Development of markets for high quality protein content and cloning/modification of triticin gene with enhanced lysine content in wheat,
 development of molecular methods for hybrid seed mustard and production of transgenic plants of tobacco with viral resistance are some salient
 achievements.  Besides, transgenic work has been carried out on banana, cabbage, mustard, mungbean and wheat for crop improvement, increased
 nutritional value, disease resistance and better shelf life.  Efforts were being made to develop transgenic in cotton and rice. A nutritionally
 important gene, AmA1 has been transferred to Potato.

14.  The Committee has been informed that India is a partner in the international rice genome-sequencing programme, with a responsibility of
 completing sequence of chromosome 11 being undertaken at south campus Delhi University and Centre for Biotechnology, IARI, New Delhi. 
 The commitment is to sequence the 10MB of chromosome in a period of five years.
 15.  Under the Integrated Nutrient Management programme several packages were successfully undertaken to facilitate judicious application of
 chemical fertilizers and adoption of microbial inoculants for various cropping systems.  An antifungal formulation for control of root rot diseases
 was developed and transferred to industry.  An area of 65,000 hectares has been covered in different agro-climatic zones and it has benefited more
 than 30,000 farmers till date.  In order to increase the efficiency of the microbial inoculants, a number of network programmes on development of
 transgenic microbial inoculants were implemented. Under Plant Tissue culture/Micro Propagation parks programme the Department achieved
 success by Tissue Culture for woody species, forest trees, horticulture and plantation crops. It was tested on Tea, Coffee and pepper.  Successful
 studies were continuing on the genetic manipulation of neem and populous, DNA fingerprinting of important clones of forest trees, re-generation
 system of mango varieties, tissue culture of rare and threatened flowering plants, transgenic virus resistant papaya and disease free citrus. 
16.      Technologies for eucalyptus, teak and bamboo have been transferred to Cadila Pharmaceuticals Ltd.  Three turnkey projects for state
 Departments have also been undertaken  for contract production.  A satellite park has been setup at Guwahati for popularization and use of
 technology. 
17.As regards the programmes under the forest trees the same need to be developed extensively with a view to increase the forest cover. 
 This in turn, would help in arresting ecological imbalances.  Besides, the technology be made available for social forestry programmes.
 
MEDICAL BIOTECHNOLOGY
18.  The Committee was informed that the transgenic mice produced at National Institute of Immunology, New Delhi would be useful in the
 development of pharmaceuticals and drugs.  Over 1.5 lakh doses of immunomodulator Leprovac have been supplied to NGO’s and hospitals for
 treatment of leprosy patients.  Further its use as an immuno-prophylactic agent was ascertained by conducting survey of vaccinee population of
 Ghatampur at Kanpur Dehat.  The survey was done by independent agencies and decoding of the results showed protection in 68% of subjects. 
 The Department has transferred a number of technologies to industry for improvements/scale up and commercialization.  Some of these were a
 Mac-ELISA system for the detection of Igm antibodies for detection of dengue virus; Igm Mac-ELISA for detection Hepatitis-A; a new
 expression system for Hepatitis-B genes with the possibility of a new recombinant Hepatitis-B vaccine technology; the ELISA based assessment
 of 4 reproductive hormones and the ELISA systems to monitor the level of alpha-fetoprotein.  The Committee was also informed that a HIV viral
 repository at National AIDS Research Institute, Pune has 91 isolates from different parts of the country.  This repository has both HIV-I and HIV-
II isolates.  A novel anti HIV glycoprotein from the first trimester placental human tissue with a molecular weight of 100 KDa has been isolated
 and found to significantly inhibit the multiplication of HIV-I strain. A novel enzyme alfa aminolevulinate dehydrogenase has been identified as a
 target for new drug development for malaria.  A new molecule to deliver anti-malarial compound has been identified.  The chromosome 10 of
 Leishmania donovani has new drug/vaccine targets like topoisomerase II, adenosine Kinase, cyclophelin and Gp 63.  Complete sequence of the
 chromosome 10 of L. donovani was being carried out for the first time in the world.  The research projects implemented in the areas of major
 infectious and non-infectious disease viz. tuberculosis, HIV,  malaria,  leishmaniasis,  cholera,  H.Pylori, dengue, tuyphoid,  cancer,  heart
 diseases  and
contraceptive vaccine showed significant progress.  Major emphasis was also given on generation of projects on oral cancer and clinical
 applications of the stem cells.
19.The Committee is constrained to observe that the leprosy vaccine developed by the National Institute of Immunology is yet to be
 included by the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare in its leprosy control programme.  The Committee has been given to understand
 that voluntary agencies have made use of 24 lakh doses of the vaccines whereas the Ministry of Health continues to import the vaccines
 instead of making use of the one developed by the National Institute of Immunology.  If it is really so, the Committee observes that it
 constitutes draining out of the precious foreign exchange from the national exchequer.  This needs to be pursued with the Ministry of
 Health on priority basis.
HUMAN GENETICS AND GENOME ANALYSIS
20.  Fourteen genetic clinics and three major projects were established for providing molecular diagnosis and counseling for the common genetic
 disorders prevalent in the country to the affected families.  About 13,000 affected families so far have been benefited from these units for genetic
 diagnosis including prenatal diagnosis and counselling for major genetic disorders. In the programme on functional genomics powerful
 computational capability for handling large scale human genome sequence data, robotic methodologies for genotyping and PCR based diagnostics
 for common genetic disorders have been developed.  A brain storming session on post-genome era was organized to discuss programmes in
 genomics.
JAI VIGYAN MISSIONS
21.  Four National Jai Vigyan Science and Technology missions covering the areas of vaccines, herbal medicines, mirror sites for genomic
 research and coffee biotechnology network were being monitored by expert committees and the Ministry for Science & Technology.  They were
 progressing as per the identified milestones.  There have been several leads in the area of vaccines, coffee and herbal product development, which
 would deliver potential products and processes.  The mirror sites established at four places for genomic studies have become operational and work
 has gained significant momentum after the announcement of human genome draft sequence.
22.The Committee commends the work done by the Department in the field of rice genome sequencing and observes that more such programmes need to be undertaken especially in crops like
 pulses which are in short supply in the country, maize, oilseeds, and other dry farming crops keeping in view the extremely varied climate, cropping patterns, variety of crops available in the
 country.

 enjoys a large asset of R&D personnel and infrastructural facilities.  Scientists and policy makers need more information and facilities for
 protecting the products of intellectual power of Indian Scientists.  As a step in this direction, a single window Biotechnology Patent Facilities Cell
 was created by the Department of Biotechnology (DBT) at the Bio-informatics Division of the Department, in July 1999.

      Creating awareness and understanding among biologists and biotechnologists, relating to patents and the challenges & opportunities in this
 area  including arranging workshops, seminars,

28.  The embryo transfer technology was being used to produce genetically superior animals for herd improvement.  Major programmes on
 developing transgenic animals were underway.  Transgenic mice expressing neomycin resistance gene, green fluorescent protein gene and

29.  The Committee has been informed that under the National Jai Vigyan mission, a DNA vaccine for preventing rabies in dogs was being

 on 24
th November 2000.  The Biotechnology Park seeks to provide opportunities for professionally qualified women to take career of remunerative self-employment through organization
 of environment friendly biotechnological enterprises. The park would provide central facilities viz. technology resourcing, training, and marketing.
32.While the Committee is satisfied with the programme related to setting up of Biotechnology Parks, it emphasizes the need for such Parks if they help the cause of development of  wasteland
 in villages which could possibly be another area of augmenting the income of farmers/women in rural areas.
BIOVILLAGE
33.  The  Committee was informed that a biovillage has been established at Morcha village, Probandar, for extension of technologies which are
 pro-poor, pro-women and pro-nature to the grass root level.  These technologies provide income generation opportunities for the targeted
 population.  In the village farmers are trained in production and use of bio-fertilizers, bio-pesticides, Modern farming  practices and cultivation of
 Marine algae seaweeds.  Cultivation  of
Medicinal and economically important plant species has also been undertaken in wasteland of the village.  A desalination unit for pure water has
 also been set up.
34.The    Committee commends the concept of Biovillage taken up by the Department.  The Committee however feels the need for more such projects being undertaken in those villages where
 chemical fertilizer is abundantly used.  Training also needs to be provided for use of the bio-fertilizers in view of their minimal impact on environment.
SERIBIOTECHNOLOGY
35.  The Committee has been informed that the Department’s efforts in developing silkworm genome were showing positive results and a
 programme was being undertaken at Centre for DNA Finger printing and Diagnostics, Hyderabad. The Department aims to produce transgenic
 silkworm cell/caterpillars and mulberry plants to produce better quality silk. Diverse silkworm strains characterized and transgenic silkworm
 lines/caterpillars are being developed. The technique has been standardized for effective degumming of silk using fungal enzyme for better   luster
 and softness of silk.

BIOINFORMATICS
37.  This programme encompasses all aspects of biological information, viz, acquisition, processing, storage, distribution, analysis and
 interpretation which combines the tools and techniques of mathematics, computer science, and biology with an aim of understanding the
 biological significance of a variety of data and dissemination of up to date information resources to researchers and development of various tools
 for biotechnology and molecular biology applications. At present 55 centres are set up under the programme to carry out Bioinformatics and R&D
 activities Internationally recognised data bases such as EMBnet, PDB, GDB, EBI and plant genome database has been established under National
 Jai Vigyan S&T Mission.  These can be utilised for genomics and R&D activities through high speed and high bandwidth network services. A
 dedicated  high speed ,high bandwidth network is being established for major centers engaged in bioinformatics  R&D and educational activities.
 A directory of industries and institutions in SAARC region has been completed and would be available on  web.
38.The Committee observes that India is one of the first countries in the world to initiate a Bioinformatics programme.  Besides, given the advantages the country has in IT sector and its
 expertise in mathematics and high knowledge base, special emphasis needs to be given to this aspect as  sustainability and dissemination of the data is necessary for the success of  plans.
 The researchers should also have the access to updated knowledge to keep themselves abreast of research elsewhere in the world.   This would help avoid duplicating the research and in
 patenting the research already conducted.
INTERNATIONAL COLLABORATION
39.  The Committee has been informed that interaction amongst scientific community was going on through bilateral  and  multilateral 
 collaboration.  India  has  joint projects  with  Switzerland,
USA, Sri Lanka, UK, Germany, Israel, France and Tunisia. In an Indo-Swedish project process for the production of lactic acid using a strain of
 lactobacillus was developed along with a biosensor system. R&D projects under Indo-US programme on Contraceptive and Reproductive Health
 Research have been implemented. Under the integrated long term programme of Indo-Russian collaboration in the biotechnology, a research and
 networking center –Indo-Russian center for Biotechnology was in the process of being established in New Delhi with a focus on research in plant
 and medical biotechnology. A new phase of Indo-Swiss collaboration in biotechnology has been agreed for implementation during 1999-2004
 with  focus on biotechnology applications in agriculture and environment  with special reference to improvement of wheat and pulses. Besides
 bilateral collaborations with Myanmar, Belarus and Israel have also been initiated.
40.  The joint working group of Indo-US vaccine Action Programmemet at NIH, USA to develop strategic plans for new programmes for the next
 decade and to develop candidate vaccines for malaria, tuberculosis and HIV in partnership with other agencies. Two potential candidate vaccines
 for rota viral diarrhoea have been developed at AIIMS, New Delhi and IISc, Bangalore and have been produced in USA for limited field trials.
41.The Committee observes that studies conducted under the bilateral cooperation should aim at research in developing drugs for diseases that are particular to our country such as  Kala-azar,
 plague, tuberculosis  & malaria etc.
AUTONOMOUS INSTITUTIONS
42.  Department of biotechnology supports research activities in various research institutions viz; Indian Institute of Immunology, National Brain
 Research centre, National Centre for Plant Genome Research, Centre for Cell Science and Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics.
CENTRE FOR DNA FINGERPRINTING AND DIAGNOSTICS (CDFD)
43.  The Department has sought an allocation of Rs.10.25 crores for the year 2001-2002 to construct an office complex with a view create an apex
 centre to guide the DNA finger printing, diagnostics and to increase its scope of research. The center was established with an aim to provide DNA
 finger printing services for crime investigation and for settling paternity disputes and (identification of biological parents) provide DNA finger
 diagnostic services.  The centre was also involved in diagnosis of cases suffering from infertility, hemophilia, fragile x, muscular dystrophy and
 other genetic disorders Asked whether the facilities available at the institute were sufficient to cope with the requirements of the increasing
 population, proportionate crime taking place in the country and cases of unnatural deaths etc.  The Committee was informed that a Memorandum
 of understanding (MOU) was signed by the centre with other state forensic laboratories so as to make them at par with the centre to handle routine
 cases on their own as part of the technology transfer.  As such there were no plans  to set up any other institution of its kind.
44.  Centre receives 5-6 cases per day and it has reinforced its diagnostics and molecular diagnostic. This is believed to be because of awareness of
 Indian population to genetic disorders.  The centre has also started a screening programme for diagnosing in born errors of metabolism for newly
 born children, and centre also provides genetic counseling to parents of affected children.
 
 
45.The Committee expresses its satisfaction with the work being done by the Centre for DNA Finger Printing and Diagnostics (CDFD) in the field of Automated Genome Analysis, Bioinformatics
 Diagnostics, DNA Fingerprinting. Instrumentation and Research in, among other areas, cancer Biology, computational Biology and Immunology etc.
46.The Committee however feels that the country’s population having touched 1020 million and as the crimes, conflicts and paternity disputes are expected to arise with more frequency the
 rising pace of population it was time to consider whether there was need to set up full fledged institutes to provide the services to the institutions and people expeditiously and with minimum of
 costs.

 national/international organisations involved in neuroscience research.  The major objectives of NBRC are to undertake basic research to
 understand function of the brain in disease and normal conditions. The centre has achieved its objectives both in setting up its main facility (intra-
mural) and its networking activities (extra-mural). Among other activities the centre also conducted an Indo-US workshop to identify areas like
 computational neuroscience, development of tools for image analysis, brain banking and neurogenetics.     Agreements were also being made for
 research cooperation and training with USA & Japan.
48.  Asked for the details of the programmes to be undertaken with the increased allocation of Rs.3.00 crores the Department informed the
 Committee  that it planned to initiate programmes in new areas of neuroscience such as system and cognitive neuroscience and neural stem cell
 research to keep pace with research world wide. Besides, NBRC , has been invited to join “Global Efforts for Development of Neuroinformatics”

1.  The financial allocation for 2001-2002 for the Department of Biotechnology is Rs.186.34 crores as against the revised allocation of  Rs.150.89 crores. The allocation of Rs.186.34
 crores, seen against the background of budgetary support provided during the year 2000-2001 represents an increase of about Rs.50 crores or about 37% (precisely 36.82%) over the
 year's amount. The committee would like to know whether the increase of about Rs.50 crores is due to the erosion in the value of money or due to inclusion of new items of work for
 which budgetary support is required.
Ans: The budget of Rs.186.34 crores allocated for the year 2001-2002 includes Rs. 175.00 crores for plan and Rs. 1 1.34 crores for non-plan activities. The increase is mainly in the
 plan budget amounting to Rs.35.00 crores over the RE of Rs.139.92 crores (plan) and Rs.50.00 crores over the BE of Rs.125.00 crores (plan) of the year 2000-2001. The new
 programmes, which will be initiated during 2001-2002, include establishment of "GEN-NET INDIA" to cure, control and care genetic disorders prevalent in the country alongwith the
 development of network programmes on human      genome      diversity    and    biochips      in   genomics      towards       gene identification/diagnostics. Comparative
 genomics, data annotation, proteomics, pharmaco genomics and work on some microbial genomics would be started. The second initiative includes  integrated approach towards
 utilization and conservation of medicinal plants for herbal drug development employing biotechnology tools and techniques. Other  programmes recently initiated such as Indian Initiative
 on Rice Genome Sequencing and activities of National Bioresource Development Board as well as  National Brain Research Centre will be implemented as per targets. There is also
 increase for Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics and Brain Research activities.
2.    It is a commendable effort on the part of DBT to have kept the non-plan expenditure at the level of Rs.1 I crores. But if one sees the allocation of Rs.1 75 crores under the plan
 expenditure, it represents an increase of 40 % over the budgetary support enjoyed by the department in the previous year. What have been the reasons for this substantial increase?
Ans: During the year 2001-2002, new programmes on Genome Research, Biotechnology of Medicinal Plants for Herbal/Drug Development and implementation of activities of recently
 initiated projects such as Indian Initiative on Rice Genome Sequencing and activities of National Bioresource Development Board as well as National Brain Research Centre will be
 undertaken utilising specifically the increased budgetary support under plan (as detailed in the answer for the question 1).

9.   The financial allocation for Biotech products and processes has  marginally been reduced by Rs.0.15 crores (Rs.11.00 crores in current year) from Rs.11.15 crores during RE and
 Rs.11.25 crores in BE stage in the year 2000-2001. With the plan to launch biotechnology based programmes especially  for women and weaker section, doesn't this reduction in
 allocation affect the progress of this endeavour and deny opportunities to major beneficiaries?
Ans: During the year 2000-01, the R.E. of Rs.2.45 crores was provided for biotechnology based programmes for women under the scheme biotech products and process development
 due to commitments for implementing the activities in the golden jubilee women biotechnology park at Chennai. The department was implementing about I 1 projects for providing
 opportunities to beneficiaries. For the financial year  (2001-2002), B.E. has been kept at Rs.1.10 crores to meet these ongoing projects and initiate few new projects for women
 empowerment and skill development. Besides, the budgetary support under programmes for rural areas  under the same scheme has been increased from an R.E. level of Rs.90.00
 lakhs during the year 2000-01 to a B.E. of Rs.2.00 crores for the financial year  2001-02 to initiate a special programme involving biotechnology interventions  in relief and rehabilitation
 of earthquake victims of Gujarat.
 
10. There is no increase in allocation for International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB)? Is it likely to affect the pace
 of research being undertaken by the centre in the current year?
Ans: Based on the discussions at Enlarged Bureau of ICGEB held in June 1998 in Rome and V meeting of Board of Governors at Triesty, Italy in September 1998 as well as request
 of additional funds for air-conditioning and P-3 facility as one time grant, an annual contribution of Rs.5.00 crores to be continued beyond 1999 till the end of 9 th plan period, under
 non-plan, was considered appropriate. This proposal was approved by the Cabinet in its meeting in August 1999 to continue contribution of Rs.5.00 crore per annum to ICGEB upto
 financial year 2001-02 and one time grant of Rs. 1. 1 9 crores for infrastructure. This amount should be sufficient to sustain the present research activities.
11.   The Department has not sought any plan allocation for BIBCOL. However, it has asked for Rs.10.96 crores under non-plan expenditure in 2000- 2001. What was the specific
 purpose for making these allocations? What is the current financial health of the unit. Any chances of its closure or disinvestments during the current year?
Ans: The Bharat Immunologicals & Biologicals Corporation Limited (BIBCOL) is a PSU formulating Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) from imported monovalent bulk since 1996.  The company
 has been registered under BIFR. The IDBI has prepared a revival plan and submitted to BIFR for final approval. The final hearing is scheduled in April 2001. During the current
 financial year the company has formulated 220 million doses of OPV and supplied to National Immunization Programme (170 million doses to UNICEF and 50 million doses to Ministry
 of Health & Family Welfare. The company has already paid Rs.16.00 crores to financial institutions  out of Rs.18.85 crores obtained from Fis as term loan. At present, the company  is
 generating revenues to sustain their regular activities. Hence, the department has not sought any plan allocation during the next financial year. The company has projected a non- plan
 expenditure of Rs.10.96 crores during financial year 2000-01 to be met form Internal and Extra Budgetary Resources  (IEBR) (Rs.7.71 crores from internal resources and Rs.3.25 crores
 as loans from outside sources). There is no such proposal for closure or disinvestments during the current financial year.
12.   The allocation made under the head "Other Scientific Research" has been substantially increased to Rs.175 crores in the current year from Rs.140.00 crores at RE stage and
 Rs.135.96 crores at BE stage. What are the details of the projects being covered under the enhanced allocation?
Ans: Under the head 'Other Scientific Research', the budget has been increased to initiate following programmes of immediate importance.
      (i)   Taking advantage of the announcement of working draft of human genome, programmes will be implemented in the areas of sequencing of
 specific pathogens relevant to the country, global gene expression studies using microarray technology, development of Single Nucleotide
 Polymorphisms (SNPS) for specific haematological disorders, programme support to Centre for Human Genetics at Bangalore,
 pharmacogenomics.
      (ii)      Integrated wheat genomic programme and functional genomic of rice will be taken up.
      (iii)A special integrated programme in collaboration with other ministries and departments on bioprospecting and conservation of medicinal
 plants towards development of new herbal drug formulations will be initiated.
      (iv)A special programme involving biotechnology interventions in relief and rehabilitation of earthquake victims of Gujarat will be taken up
 under programmes for rural areas.
      (v)  Building construction and new research activities under National Brain Research Centre will be further taken up.
     (vi)          Completion of animal house facility and establishment of technology incubation facility at National Institute of Immunology will be undertaken.

R E P O R T
      The Department of Ocean Development was created in July, 1981 within the Cabinet Secretariat directly under the charge of the
 Prime Minister. In March, 1982 it became a separate Department and has since been functioning as a nodal Department for
 organizing, coordinating and promoting ocean development activities in the country, in line with the Ocean Policy Statement of 1982.
 The programmes pursued by the Department over the years have also kept pace with developments World over and addressed
 National needs and issues.
     The activities of the Department are directed towards:
(i)        Technology Development Programmes for future applications with strategic, industrial and economic significance.
(ii)        Societal Programmes with direct/indirect benefit for the community by technology applications and pilot project
 demonstration with the participation of the community for their socio-economic prosperity, and for coastal area
 development.
(iii)       Marine Resources Programmes for exploration of marine living and non-living resources, techno-economic studies to
 evolve strategies for sustainable exploration and utilisation, and resource enhancement.
(iv)       Multi-institutional and multi-disciplinary Polar Science Programmes and Antarctic Expeditions with scientific and
 geo-political significance.
(v)       Capacity Building Programme towards self-reliance through basic scientific research in ocean sector, human resource
 development and establishing Centres of Excellence in academic institutions.
(vi)                 Creation of public awareness on the potential and uses of ocean.
 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 2001-02
2.   The   Secretary informed the Committee that the total budgetary  demand for the year 2001-02 is as follows:
                    Plan          - Rs.142.00 crores
                    Non-Plan  - Rs.26.80 crores
                    Total       - Rs.168.80 crores
2.1The plan outlay for 2001-02 has been fixed at Rs.142.00 crores, which is Rs. 07.00 crore more than that of  2000-01 level, of which
 Rs.43.00 crore is meant for the delineation of outer limits of Continental Shelf and the remaining Rs.99.00 crore for the other Plan
 schemes.
3.   The Committee was apprised that the approved outlay for the Antarctic Research was Rs.20.00 crores,  which  would be given as
 Grants-in-aid to National Centre for Antarctic & Ocean Research (NCAOR) for launching the 21
st  Scientific Expedition to
 Antarctica, carrying out scientific experiments, maintenance of the permanent research station “Maitri” at Antarctica and operation
 and manning of the NCAOR. 
4.   In the case of Poly Metallic Nodules (PMN) programme, an outlay of Rs.17.30crore has been provided. This includes Rs.0.05 crore
 for survey and exploration, Rs.0.25 crore for the Environmental Impact Assessment (both under the S&T component), Rs.1.00 crore
 for mining and research and development, Rs.5.00 crore for wet leasing of Sidorenko (Russian vessel), Rs.5.00 crore for development
 of Unmanned Submersibles under a joint programme with the Institute of Russian Academy of Sciences and Rs.6.00 crore for
 metallurgy technology development. The Secretary informed the Committee that the Technology Demonstration pilot plant for
 extraction of metals from Poly Metallic Nodules at Hindustan Zinc Limited (HZL), which was initially to be commissioned by
 October, 2000 will now be commissioned by May, 2001.
5.   In the mission mode programmes of National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) including Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion
 (OTEC), an outlay of Rs.13.30 crores has been provided. The Expenditure Finance Committee has approved an outlay of Rs.35.25
 crore for OTEC programme to be implemented during the Ninth Five year Plan. The pilot plant which was expected to be
 commissioned off Tuticorin coast in September-October, 2000, is now expected to be commissioned during the current financial year,
 for which a sum of Rs.4.21 crore has been provided. The provision includes Rs.2.96 crore for meeting the increase in the cost estimate
 for evaporator and condenser for OTEC plant, owing to increase in the area  by almost 50% of the original area of the heat exchanger. 
 NIOT is also exploring the possibility of having a tie-up with some of the agencies involved in the power sector for technical and
 financial collaboration, for commercial operation once the pilot plant operation becomes successful.
6.   The Secretary informed the Committee that an outlay of Rs.43 crores has been provided for the Delineation of Continental Shelf in

 2001-02. Since India ratified the UN convention on the Law of the Sea in 1995, the claim for extending the outer limits of our
 continental shelf beyond 200 nautical miles Exclusive Economic Zone has to be made before 2005. The time frame for carrying out
 the bathymetric and seismic surveys and preparing necessary documents to submit to the Commission on the Limits of Continental
 Shelf is 5 years.
6.1Considering this, the Government approved the scheme with an outlay of Rs.47.46 crore for implementation over a period of three
 years ending 2000-01.  The outlay was augmented to Rs.4.00 crore at RE level from Rs.0.50 crore at BE stage for 1999-2000.  The
 remaining amount of Rs.43 crore has been provided in 2000-01 budget. However, the contract for carrying out the bathymetric and
 seismic surveys couldn’t be finalised during 2000-01 and hence at the RE stage, the provision of Rs.43.00 crore was surrendered. This
 amount has now been provided for in 2001-2002. The National Centre for Antarctic & Ocean Research (NCAOR), Goa is
 coordinating the implementation of this programme.
7.   An outlay of Rs.2.96 crore is proposed for  Marine Living Resources Programme.  Besides, an amount of Rs.2.20 crore is proposed
 to be allocated for the ongoing Drugs from Sea programme. During the year 2001-2002, a provision of Rs.1.15 crore has been made
 for Marine Non-Living Resources such as Bengal and Nicobar Fan (BENFAN). The Committee was also informed that an outlay of
 Rs.19.70 crores has been provided for the Ocean Observation & Information Services. Out of this, the provision for the Indian
 National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) at Hyderabad is Rs.7.25 crore and for the National Data Buoy programme
 and the other Ocean Observing System programmes, a sum of Rs.9.25 crore has been provided.
 
8.   An outlay of Rs.4.05 crore and Rs.3.94 crore has been made for Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction Systems (COMAPS)
 and Coastal Research Vessel (CRV) respectively during the Annual Plan 2001-02. An outlay of Rs.6.50 crore has been provided for
 2000-2001 for the Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management (ICMAM) Programme. 
9.   In line with the guidelines provided by the Island Development Authority the Department of Ocean Development have made a
 provision of Rs.0.75 crore for Island Development.  This is a coastal community programme implemented through National Institute
 of Ocean Technology (NIOT), by which viable technologies for enhancement of marine living resources would be developed and
 disseminated to the island community for their benefit.
10.The Department projected an outlay of Rs.157.21 crore for Annual Plan 2001-02 to the Planning commission.  However, the
 Planning Commission has restricted the outlay to Rs.142.00 crore.  Consequently the Department has rescheduled some of the
 initiatives, particularly the unmanned submersibles programme to 2001-2002.
12.The Details of budgetary projections for the programmes of the Department of Ocean Development during the year 2001-02 are
 given at Annexure-I and comparative figures in terms of provision actually made/ approved and actually utilised during 1998-99,
 1999-2000 and 2000-2001 are given at Annexure-II.
13.Asked whether the total financial outlay (plan as well as non-plan) of Rs.168.80 crores would suffice against Rs.158 crores in the
 BE of the last year, the Department has stated that it had prepared plan proposed for Rs.157.21 crores but after discussion with the
 Planning Commission, the plan outlay was fixed at Rs.142 crores which has forced the Department to reduce the outlay for the
 “Antarctic Expedition & Polar Science”, “Poly Metallic Nodules” , “Coastal and Marine Area Management”, Ocean Observation &
 Information Services”, and “Marine Research and Capacity Building” programmes.
14. The Committee observes that in view of considerable reduction in the Budgetary support at RE level last year, it should be possible
 for the Department to manage with the reduced budgetary support this year.  To that end the Committee brings on record the
 assurance given by the Department in reply to Question 1 of the Questionnaire  (See Appendix) that the present outlay will not hold
 up the execution of any programme”.
15.  In the context of delay in the Commissioning the Technology Demonstration Pilot Plant for extraction of metals from Poly
 Metallic Nodules at Hindustan Zinc Ltd., at Udaipur, which was to be commissioned in October, 2000 and the Pilot Plant which was
 expected to be commissioned off Tuticorin coast in September-October, 2000, the Committee observes that such delays result in cost
 escalations.  Besides, they reflect on the Departments’ efficiency to plan things meticulously.   Such delays need to be avoided.

 of Continental Shelf (CLCS) by June 2005. If delineation is properly undertaken, India would be in a position to make exclusive claim
 on the continental shelf. This could provide India with an area of more than 1 million sq. km of continental shelf beyond the EEZ. In
 case India does not submit claim before the CLCS, the continental shelf beyond 200 nautical miles would lie in international waters
 and India would have the same claim to it as other members of the international community.
24.The class of work envisaged in establishing the claim is new for India. The Technical & Scientific Guidelines were issued in May
 1999 about a year behind schedule. The Guidelines as formulated need careful interpretation. The terms used in the Guidelines often

 technical experts to ensure that India does not lose available opportunity.
25.The United Nations Convention on Law of the Sea provides two means of delineating the Shelf to India and Sri Lanka. The two
 countries can either choose to use Article 76 which applies to all countries signatory to the Convention or Annex 11 to the Final Act to
 the Third United Nations Conference on Law of the Sea which applies to just the two countries. There are advantages and
 disadvantages in using either of the provisions and it is necessary to put in place a carefully thought out strategy that best serves
 India's interests. This work is close to completion.

 temperature, current, salinity, upwelling, potential fishing zone information, coastal maps, etc., to support coastal and off-shore
 developmental activities and for furthering quality oceanographic research. The OOIS was aimed at development of a system for Ocean
 State Forecast, on experimental basis by 2001-02.
45.1 The programme consists of four major components viz. Ocean Observing Systems, Ocean Information Services, Ocean Dynamics and
 Modelling and Satellite Coastal and Oceanographic Research.  
45.2  The  project consists of three sub-projects viz., National Data Buoy Programme(NDBP), Sea Level observation and Drifting buoy
 and other Observing systems.
46.The National Data Buoy Programme was being implemented by National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT), Chennai.  The
 programme envisages assembly, deployment, operation and maintenance of state-of-the-art technology data buoys.  Under this
 programme, a set of 12 met-ocean data buoys have been deployed in the coastal and offshore of India for acquiring, surface
 meteorological and upper ocean parameters.  The buoys were equipped with state-of-the-art sensors for accurate measurement of winds,
 waves, currents, atmospheric pressure, atmospheric temperature, sea surface temperature, dissolved oxygen, chlorophyll, radioactivity,
 hydrocarbon and turbidity.
46.1 The Secretary informed the Committee that NDBP carried out regular and emergency maintenance of data buoys whenever required.
 During the year under report, NDBP has accomplished 18 deployments, 9 retrievals and 1 in-situ servicing of buoys.  The features for
 buoys have been improved to be tamper proof.  A shore station was commissioned at NIOT for retrieval, processing, analysis and storage
 of the data from the buoys.  The data was being disseminated daily at 3 GMT to India Meteorological Department and Coast Guard has
 contributed to the process of the forecast of cyclones in the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea.
47.The programme under Drifting Buoys Programme envisages deployment of a series of drifting buoys, expendable bathythermographs
 (XBTs) and current  meter arrays for augmentation of in situ oceanographic measurements.  During the IX plan period, about 50 drifting
 buoys, 3 current meter arrays, and 900 XBTs would  be deployed under the programme.  The data from the buoys is transmitted online
 using CLS-ARGOS satellite primarily for validation of satellite sensors besides its contribution towards understanding the oceanographic
 processes around India.
48.The Committee was informed that under the Sea Level Observation project, 10 modern tide gauge stations were established at Mumbai,
 Porbandar, Goa, Kochi, Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Paradip, Kavaratti, Machlipatnam and Tuticorin for systematic and accurate monitoring
 of the tide levels to assess the long-term variations in the mean sea levels.  The data from those tide gauges are collected regularly and
 archived at National Tide Data Centre at Survey of India, Dehradun. Based on the sea level data collected along the Indian coast, a
 numerical model has been constructed to simulate circulation in the Northern Indian Ocean.
 
 
 
49.While the Committee notes with satisfaction that the programmes under the Ocean Observation Information Service  have been
 successful, it observes that  the indigenisation of Data buoy technology and Operation and maintenance of 12 data buoy system by
 National Data Buoy Programme is yet to be achieved. The Committee observes that the upgradation of existing tide gauge network both in
 terms of software and sensors redeployment of existing current meter and deployment of new current meter array along the equator would
 take place during this financial year. Similarly the Committee would  appreciate if  under the  programme Ocean Dynamics and Modelling
 (INDOMOD), validation of Coupled Atmospheric Ocean Model (CAOM) to provide forcing parameter for ocean general circulation
 model and sensitivity test for CAOM for prediction of storm surges associated with tropical cyclone along the Indian coast would be
 conducted and validated. The experiments to determine the sensitivity for development of hybrid coupled model for prediction of Indian
 monsoon regions have  also to be achieved

QUESTION 2
Over the years, the Department has been pleading for more funds and the Committee had taken into consideration the fact that for continuity of its long term
 programmes/schemes, the Department requires extra budgetary support but the actual expenditure in the year 2000-2001 being Rs.51.83 crores less than the budgetary
 allocation it is felt that the Department has not meticulously followed the programme to ensure full utilization of the funds. What are the comments of the Department?
ANSWER 2
The shortfall indicated above is on account of reduction in the Plan and Non- Plan outlays.
NON-PLAN
As indicated above, the Non-Plan outlay was reduced from Rs. 23 crores at the BE stage to Rs. 19.99 crores at RE stage as an economy measure. This was
 despite the Department's need for additional funds for the operation of its two research vessels- Sagar Kanya and Sagar Sampada.
 
PLAN
In relation to Plan, the outlay stands reduced from Rs. 135 crores at the BE level to Rs. 86.18 crores  at RE stage. Of the above reduction in Plan expenditure, the
 reduction of Rs. 43 crores was on account of the Department's inability to implement the programme on Delineation of the Continental Shelf. The remaining shortfall of
 Rs. 5.82 crores is on account of the general need for economy.
In relation to the programme to delineate the Continental shelf it would be noted that India has to submit claim to the Commission on the Limits of Continental Shelf
 by June 2005. If delineation is properly undertaken, India would be in a position to make exclusive claim on the continental shelf. This could provide
India with an area of more than I million sq. km of continental shelf beyond the EEZ. In case India does  not submit claim before the CLCS, the continental shelf
 beyond 200 nautical miles would lie in international waters and India would have the same claim to it as other members of the international community.
The class of work envisaged in establishing the claim is new for India. The Technical & Scientific Guidelines were issued in May 1999 about a year behind
 schedule. The Guidelines as formulated need careful interpretation. The terms used in the Guidelines  often have a legal interpretation different from the normal technical
 usage. The proper meaning of the terms has to be jointly decided by legal and technical experts to ensure that India does not lose available opportunity.
The United Nations Convention on Law of the Sea provides two means of delineating the Shelf to India and Sri Lanka. The two countries can either choose to use
 Article 76 which applies to all countries signatory to the Convention or Annex 11 to the Final Act to the Third United Nations Conference on Law of the Sea which
 applies to just the two countries. There are advantages and disadvantages in using either  of the provisions and it is necessary to put in place a carefully thought out
 strategy that best serves India's interests. This work is close to completion. Substantial progress has been achieved in collating the available seismic and bathymetric
 data to define with greater precision than before the likely area of  claim. The Indian baselines are also in the final stages of promulgation by the Ministry of External
 Affairs. It is hoped that during 2001-02 significant progress will be achieved through dialogue with Sri Lanka and through physical surveys.

ANSWER 4
India has been at the forefront of the Poly Metallic Nodules Programme since the early eighties. In 1987, India was accorded the status of Registered Pioneer
 Investor and allotted 1,50,000 sq. km. of mining site in the Central Indian Ocean. India was the first country to be so registered. India's achievement is a matter of pride
 not only for the country but also for the developing world.
     As 'Pioneer Investor', India has the following major obligations:
(a)       it shall incur expenditure annually in the development of technologies for exploration of pioneer areas and exploitation of the manganese nodules;
(b)       it shall provide training to UN nominated technical personnel from developing countries,
(c)       it shall arrange for transfer of technology to the International seabed Authority whenever the necessity arises;
When India first undertook the programme it was clear that there would be no immediate commercial benefits. It was however decided to go in for the programme in

     In relation to "mining" the following were achieved:
(a)       demonstration of the shallow bed mining system for manoeuverability of the crawler system was done in October, 2000. Tests for sampling of slurry
 through a riser hose from 410 m water depth were done earlier.
(b)       detailed engineering and specification of a mining complex module of 25,000 tonnes/year capacity for 6000 m depth has been carried out jointly by
 NIOT, Chennai and IKS, University of Seigen, Germany.
(c)       upgraded version of ROV developed by Central Mechanical Engineering Research Institute,Durgapur is ready for a test in open sea up to a depth of
 250 m.
In relation to "extraction" the processing plant being constructed by the Hindustan Zinc Ltd. at Udaipur is in the final phase of completion. The nodules required for
 processing have been collected. The R&D activities to optimise extraction efficiencies are progressing well.
     The cruise to the Central Indian Ocean Basin to study the progress of re- colonisation of benthic organisms, disturbed in an earlier experiment, has Laen planned
 and will be shortly undertaken under the "environmental" component.
QUESTION 5
The Department in coordination with National Institute of Ocean Technology, Chennai and Institute of Konstruction (IKS), University of Seigen, Germany has been
 able to develop shallow bed mining system at 410 mts. off Tuticorin Coast. The Committee would like to know the steps taken to ensure continuous operation,
 manoeuverability, etc. at a shallower depth of an integrated mining system for operation at 6000 mts.
ANSWER 5
A shallow bed mining system consisting of crawler, suction cutter pump and riser has been designed,  developed and tested jointly by National Institute of Ocean
 Technology, Chennai and Institute of Konstruction (IKS), University of Seigen, Germany. The present  system was designed for sand mining since no nodules are
 available in shallow depths. The technology developed is being spun off to permit sand dredging near river mouths and to exploit placer mineral deposits.
On the basis of expertise and experience gained, an integrated nodule mining system would be developed for 6000 m depth in two phases. The work would involve
 modification and re-design of some of the existing components to develop a mining system consisting of crawler, collector, crusher and riser.
As a first stage, the integrated system would be demonstrated at a water depth of 500 m. In the next stage after successful testing, the system would be proved at
 6000 metres water depth.
QUESTION 6

 crores allocated in the budget estimates and Rs.16.41 crores in the revised estimates for the year 2000-2001. The amount is less by Rs.3.11 crores than what was
 sought in the revised estimates (Rs.16.41 crores) for 2000-2001. Whether the reduced allocation will affect any of the activities?
 
ANSWER 6
The grants-in-aid of Rs.13.30 crores proposed for NIOT during 2001-02 is less by Rs.3.11 crores as  compared to the RE of Rs.16.41 crores for 2000-01. The
 reduction was planned on the basis that the Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) project would be substantially complete during the current financial year. An
 outlay of Rs. 4 crores in 2001-02 was thus planned for the OTEC project as against the outlay of Rs. 10 crores during the current financial year.
Unfortunately there have been so i.e. set backs in advancing the OTEC project. The pipeline system for the project after deployment drifted. The loss of components
 is being assessed. Before the pipeline system is re-deployed the strategy earlier envisaged would have to be re-assessed. Further it may be necessary to acquire a
 vessel with heavy lifting and winching capability to ensure proper deployment. It is likely  that additional funds for the programme would have to be provided in the year
 2001-02. The exact quantum would be determined only after a full assessment exercise.
The outlay for the other mission projects of NIOT like Wave Energy, Mining Technology, Coastal Engineering, Marine Instrumentation have not been reduced.
 Similarly, schemes/projects of the department entrusted to NIOT such as Coastal Research Vessels, National Data Buoy Programme and Island Development Programme

QUESTION 7
The budgetary allocation for the programme "Coastal Ocean Monitoring & Prediction System (COMAPS)" for 2001-2002 for Rs.4.05 crores which is almost twice the
 Budget Estimates for the year 2000-2001 (i.e. Rs.2.05 crores).   What are the details of the work carried out under the programme last year and what are the new
 areas proposed to be covered during the year for which an enhanced allocation is sought?
ANSWER7
During the year 2000-2001 for which the budget requirement of Rs.2.05 crores has been allocated, work carried out include monitoring pollution at 77 locations along
 with 25 hotspots database development and physical oceanographic studies to understand the diffusion and dispersion characteristics at 2 locations. During the year
 2001-2002, while the monitoring and database development programme will be continued, the hotspots will be more intensively monitored. The proposed locations for
 physical oceanographic studies will be increased to four. This leads to a financial requirement of Rs.4.05 crores.
QUESTION 8
Under the programme "Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction System" (COMAPS) after monitoring level of various marine
 pollutants in the coastal and offshore waters, 32 locations have been identified as hot spots. What steps the Department to eliminate/check
 marine pollutants at these hot spots has initiated? What steps have been taken for evolving a coordination mechanism between Department
 of Ocean Development and respective State Pollution Control Boards for continued check on marine pollution levels and utilise the data
 generated through Geographical Information System (GIS) to achieve desired results?
 
ANSWER  8
The Department of Ocean Development takes up scientific monitoring of pollution at different locations. The responsibility to control pollution in the hotspots rests with
 the State Governments through the State Pollution Control Boards. The data collected is routinely made available to the Pollution Control Boards and periodically
 discussed with them. Any significant increase in pollutants at a particular location is brought to the notice of the Central Pollution Control Board and the concerned State
 Pollution Control Board for control as well as remedial actions.
The Department of Ocean Development have constituted a Steering Committee under the Chairmanship of Chairman, Central Pollution Control Board, New Delhi with
 members from all the coastal State Pollution Control Boards to facilitate coordination as. well as  analysis of results obtained under the COMAPS programme. The GIS
 based Information system containing COMAPS data is under development by the National Institute of Oceanography, Goa.
At the national level the Ministry of Environment & Forests, Department of Ocean Development, Ministry of Shipping, Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas and
 Ministry of Defence deal with marine pollution.
QUESTION 9
What steps have been taken for evolving coordination mechanism between Department of Ocean Development and other concerned Departments like Department of
 Animal Husbandry & Dairying or Biotechnology to achieve the objective of Marine Living Resources (MLR) Programme?
ANSWER 9
Assessment of Marine Living Resources is a programme' initiated by the Department during the IX Plan period. The programme was evolved after detailed
 consultations with the bodies of the Ministry of agriculture such as the ICAR (CMFRI Kochi, CIFT Kochi, CIFE Mumbai), the Fishery Survey of India, the National
 Institute of Oceanography and Maritime Universities (Cochin University of Science & Technology and Andhra University). The programme is being implemented with the
 active participation of the above Institutions. The progress/ achievements of the projects are monitored regularly by the Task Forces of each project constituted by the
 department and also by the department's Scientific Advisory Committee on MLR, which has representatives from various Ministries and Universities.
Secretary, DOD is also the Chairman of the Group on Marine Bioresources formed as per the recommendations  of the Steering Committee of the National Sio-
resources Board and coordinated by the Department of Biotechnology. This Department is also represented on the Expert Group set up by the Department of
 Biotechnology for establishment of a Marine Biotechnology Application Centre.

 2000-2001. VVith an increase of Rs.20 lakhs only wi the Department be able to concentrate its efforts towards the transfer c technology for commercialization of drugs to

Exploratory work:

         Systematic exploration of the entire coastline and collections made from deep sea as well for identification of more flora and fauna having potential for

ANSWER 11
The allocation of Rs.75.00 lakhs under the Island Development Programme for 2001-2002 is for implementation of the Programme entitled "Ocean Science and
 Technology for Islands".
The major activity under the Island Development Programme is essentially lobster resource enhancement and transfer of this technology to island and coastal
 communities so that they may benefit economically. The activity involves technology for fattening of lobsters, biochemical analysis of lobsters and live feeds, breeding
 larval rearing and sea ranching of lobsters. The revised budgetary support of Rs-0.76 crores is adequate to meet the requirement of this Programme and no work will be
 affected. The Shore to Fishing Vessel Communication System implemented by  the DOD was only to demonstrate the technology Of communication to the coastal
 fishermen for ensuring their safety at sea. The Fisheries Division under the Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairy Development is the nodal Ministry for this
 purpose. The Ministry of Agriculture is believed to be initiating programmes for upgrading the mechanised fishing sector in the country by  providing them with
