Moreover, diversity has an insurance value, for it widens the range of environmental conditions under which different species can
 perform key ecological and economic functions. India is endowed with a rich biodiversity, as the country is well spread out in a
 wide variety of climatic zones and habitats that range from tropical rainforests to alpine vegetation, and from temperate forests to
 coastal wetlands. Eastern Himalayas and Western Ghats are two of world's 18 biodiversity hotspots, where bulk of Earth's plants
 and animals are found. India is one of the twelve mega-biodiversity areas of the world with over 45,000 wild species of plants and
 77,000 wild species of animals on record.
6.   India's rich biodiversity that exists today is estimated to be the result of over three and half million years of evolution, which
 involved speciation, migration, plate tectonics, natural holocausts, extinction and of late the human influences, interventions and
 disturbances. But during the last century, biodiversity has been drastically falling due to indiscriminate rise in human activities in
 and around forests, wetlands, rivers and oceans.
7.   There are fewer varieties of wild plants and animals today than a few decades before, and the lost varieties are gone forever. A
 high degree of endemism makes the Indian biodiversity particularly vulnerable to extinction. In last few decades, at least 50 percent
 of India’s forests have been cut down, 70 percent of its water bodies have been polluted, its grasslands cultivated and its coasts
 degraded. In addition, hunting, overexploitation, poisoning by pesticides, excessive botanical and zoological collection,
 displacement by exotic varieties and a host of other activities have taken a heavy toll of biodiversity. Already, 23 species, which
 include cheetah, the lesser one-horned rhino, and pink-headed duck, have become extinct in India, and many more species of plants
 and animals might have vanished without anyone noticing them. Nearly 750 species of plants and animals appear to be on the verge
 of extinction and the Gangetic river dolphin, Red Panda, Lion tailed macaque and the Bengal tiger are some of the highly
 endangered animals in the country today.
8.   Indiscriminate and illegal trade in wild plants and animals, combined with ecologically insensitive development projects,
 explosive growth in human population and the resultant pressure on the natural resources, are the main reasons of chronic
 biodiversity loss in India during last few decades. Specific causes have always varied with ecosystems. Even after independence,
 forests continued to be plundered in the country on a large-scale by the industries in construction, furniture making, paper & pulp,
 mining and textiles, until very recently when most of the remaining forest cover in India has come under the protection of national
 parks and wildlife sanctuaries. An important cause of habitat destruction in the Eastern Himalayan states like Sikkim and Arunachal
 Pradesh is jhum, or shifting cultivation, which is practised in 70% of the land in the region. Some experts believe that given
 sufficient area to operate, and long enough fallow periods, jhum cultivation can be sustainable. However, population pressures have
 led to a shortening of the fallow cycle, which has made this form of cultivation totally unsustainable. The Forest Survey of India has
 recently estimated that 57% of the forests have been lost due to shifting cultivation.
9.   Human interference has intensified a natural process like siltation to a degree where it has become a major threat to the wetlands
 in India. The Dal lake receives 80 000 tonnes of silt from Talbal Nalla every year, while the Chilka lake has been shrinking by
 roughly 1.5 square kilometres every year since 1925 because of siltation and the reclamation of marginal areas. Another process
 affecting wetlands is eutrophication the process by which a body of water becomes either naturally or by pollution, rich in dissolved
 nutrients and often shallow with a seasonal deficiency in dissolved oxygen.  Chilika lake in Orissa, for instance, is infested  with the
 weed Potamogeton pectinatus as a result of eutrophication of its water from the fertilizer run-offs regularly flowing in from the
 surrounding farmlands. Further, intensive fishing in rivers, lakes and seas can reduce fish populations to such an extent that they are
 no longer able to regenerate a viable number for their continued survival. The best example of this is the whale shark, which is now
 being mercilessly caught in most coastal regions of India for both eating and its fins, which command a huge price in the
 international markets.
10.  Biodiversity is India's real wealth and its resource base determines and ensures this country's survival and growth. Therefore,
 conserving and protecting this natural endowment is our primary necessity. Historically, our culture and civilization evolved and
 edified around this immense natural wealth. Our present population, with nearly 80% still directly dependent on agriculture and
 forests, cannot afford to be different.

 complement the existing laws.  He also expressed his concern over non-inclusion of Biological components from the Agriculture,
 Forestry or Fishery in the Bill.   He was of the view that the Bill did not answer as to who decides as to what was sustainable?  The
 National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) couldn’t decide for every area.  So State Biodiversity Board (SBB) should be empowered to
 decide in consultation with the Biodiversity Management Committee (BMC) created by local bodies i.e. panchayats, municipalities
 etc.  what was sustainable.  The question then arose whether BMCs would be technically qualified to decide what was ecologically
 sustainable use of biodiversity and whether it would be able to enforce that sustainable use and in the process forego revenue and
 also earn the ire of their own people who would be out to exploit the biological resources for not just personal bonafide use but for
 commercial purposes?  If not, what could be the safeguards?  “Sustainable use” means the use of biological resources after
 ascertaining on a scientific basis the harvestable   surplus of   biological   resources  in  a   given  ecosystem  after  ensuring  that  
 the productivity and ecological security of the said ecosystem, biome and biological resources were maintainable at the optimum
 level on a long term basis and also ensure that in the harvesting and removal of such harvestable surplus no adverse impact was
 caused on other biota or the land in terms of Clause 7 of the Bill.  He submitted before the Committee that it should be omitted.  It
 was a totally impracticable and indeed an absurd provision.  As agriculture, fisheries, horticulture, animal husbandry etc. were also
 commercial utilization of biological resources as defined under Clause (2)b, no person who was not a local could cultivate crops,
 grow fruit, do animal husbandry or commercial fishing, establish an atta chakki or do any research in biological sciences without
 giving prior intimation to the concerned State Biodiversity Board.  This section was not simply implementable but would also cause
 hardship and corruption.

THE BIOLOGICAL DIVERSITY BILL, 2000
A
BILL
To   provide    for   conservation  of  Biological  Diversity,  sustainable use  of   
      its  components  and  equitable sharing   of   the  benefits  arising   out  of      
     the   use  of  biological resources and  for matters connected  therewith or  
    incidental  thereto.
 
        WHEREAS India is rich in biological diversity and associated traditional and contemporary
 knowledge system relating thereto;
AND WHEREAS India is a party of the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity
 signed at Rio de Janeiro on the 5th day of June 1992;
AND WHEREAS the said Convention came into force on the                   29 th December, 1993;
AND WHEREAS the said Convention reaffirms the sovereign rights of the State over their
 biological resources;
AND W HEREAS the said Convention has the main objective of conservation of biological
 diversity, sustainable use of its components and fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising
 out of utilization of genetic resources;
AND WHEREAS it is considered necessary to provide for conservation, sustainable utilization
 and equitable sharing of benefits arising out of utilization of genetic resources and also to give
 effect to the said Convention;
BE   it  enacted  by Parliament  in the  Fifty-first Year of  the  Republic of India as follows:
CHAPTER I
PRELIMINARY
1. (1) This Act may be called the Biological Diversity Act, 2000.
(2) It extends to the whole of India.
(3) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification
 in the Official Gazette, appoint:
Provided that different dates may be appointed for different provisions of this Act and any
 reference in any such provision to the commencement of this Act shall be construed as a
 reference to the coming into force of that provision.
2. In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires -
(a)
    "benefit claimers" means the conservers of biological resources their by-products,
 creators and holders of knowledge and information relating to the use of such biological
 resources, innovations and practices associated with such use and application;
 (b) "biological diversity" means the variability among living organisms from all sources and
 the ecological complexes of which they are part and includes diversity within species or between
 species and of eco-systems;

 (c) "biological resources" means plants, animals and micro organisms or parts thereof, their
 genetic material and by-products with actual or potential use or value but does not include human
 genetic material;
 (d) "bio-survey and bio-utilization" means survey or collection of species, sub-species,
 genes, components and extracts of biological resource for any purpose and includes
 characterization, inventorisation and bioassay;
 (e) "Chairperson" means the Chairperson of the National Biodiversity Authority or, as the
 case may be, of the State Biodiversity Board;
 (f) "equitable benefit sharing" means sharing of benefits as determined by the National
 Biodiversity Authority under section 21;
 (g) "local bodies" means Panchayats and Municipalities, by whatever name called, within the
 meaning of clause (1) of article 243B and clause (1) of article 243Q of the Constitution and in the
 absence of any Panchayats or Municipalities, institutions of self-government constituted under
 any Central Act or State Act;
 (h) 
"member means member of the National Biodiversity Authority or a State Biodiversity
 Board and includes the Chairperson;
 (i) "National Biodiversity Authority" means the National Biodiversity Authority established
 under section 8;
 (j) "prescribed" means prescribed by rules made under this Act;
 (k) "regulations" means regulations made under this Act;
       (l) "research" means study or systematic investigation of any biological resource or
 technological application, that uses biological systems, living organisms or derivatives thereof to
 make or modify products or processes for any use;
 (m) "State Biodiversity Board" means the State Biodiversity Board established under section
 22;
 (n) "sustainable use" means the use of components of biological diversity in such manner
 and at such rate that does not lead to the long-term decline of the biological diversity thereby
 maintaining its potential to meet the needs and aspirations of present and future generations.

 integrate the conservation and sustainable use of biological diversity into relevant sectoral or
 cross-sectoral plans, programmes and policies.

 likely to have adverse effect on biological diversity, with a view to avoid or minimise such
 effects and where appropriate provide for public participation in such assessment;
(ii) to regulate, manage or control the risks associated with the use and release of living
 modified organisms resulting from biotechnology likely to have adverse impact on the
 conservation and sustainable use of biological diversity and human health.

 people relating to biological diversity, as recommended by the National Biodiversity Authority
 through such measures, which may include registration of such knowledge at the local, state or
 national levels, and other measures for protection, including sui generis system.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
Biodiversity encompasses the variety of all life on earth. India is one of the 12 mega
 biodiversity countries of the world. With only 2.5% of the land area, India already accounts for
 7.8% of the recorded species of the world. India is equally rich in traditional and indigenous
 knowledge, both coded and informal.
2. India is a Party of the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992). The main objectives of the
 Convention are:
(i) Conservation of biological diversity;
(ii) Sustainable use of its components;
(iii) Fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising out of utilisation of genetic resources.
 
3. Recognizing the sovereign rights of States to use their own biological resources, the
 Convention expects the Parties to facilitate access to genetic resources by other Parties for
 environmentally sound purposes subject to national legislation and on mutually agreed upon
 terms (Articles 3 and 15). Article 8(j) of the Convention recognizes contributions of local and
 indigenous communities to the conservation and sustainable utilisation of biological diversity

4. Biodiversity is a multi-disciplinary subject involving diverse sectoral activities and actions. The
 stakeholders in biological diversity include the Central Government, State Government,
 institutions of local self-government, scientific and technical institutions, experts, non-
governmental organizations, industry, etc. One of the major challenges before India lies in
 adopting an instrument which helps realise the objectives of equitable sharing of benefits
 enshrined in the Convention on Biological Diversity.
 
5. After an extensive and intensive consultation process involving the stakeholders, the Central
 Government has decided to bring a legislation with the following salient features: -
 
(i) to regulate access to biological resources of the country with the purpose of
 securing equitable share in benefits arising out of the use of biological resources;
 and associated knowledge relating to biological resources;
(ii) to conserve and sustainably use biological diversity;
(iii) to respect and protect knowledge of local communities related to biodiversity;
(iv) to secure sharing of benefits with local people as conservers of biological
 resources and holders of knowledge and information relating to the use of
 biological resources;
(v) conservation and development of areas important from the standpoint of
 biological diversity by declaring them as biological diversity heritage sites;
(vi) protection and rehabilitation of threatened species;
(vii) involvement of institutions of self-government in the broad scheme of the
 implementation of the Act through constitution of committees.
6. The proposed legislation primarily addresses the issue concerning access to genetic resources
 and associated knowledge by foreign individuals, institutions or companies, and equitable sharing
 of benefits arising out of the use of these resources and knowledge to the country and the people.
 In order to safeguard the interests of the local people, vaid and hakims and to allow research by
 Indian citizens within the country, the following exceptions are proposed: -
(i) Free access to biological resources for use within India for any purpose other
 than commercial use for Indian people.
(ii) Use of biological resources by vaids and hakims.
(iii) Free access to the Indian citizens to use biological resources within the country
 for research purposes.
(iv) Collaborative research through government sponsored or government approved
 institutions subject to overall policy guidelines and approval of the Central
 Government
.
 7. It is proposed to have National Biodiversity Authority, State Biodiversity Boards and
 Biodiversity Management Committees.
(a) The National Biodiversity Authority will deal with matters relating to requests
 for access by foreign individuals, institutions or companies, and all matters relating
 to transfer of results of research to any foreigner; imposition of terms and
 conditions to secure equitable sharing of benefits and approval for seeking any form
 of Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs) in or outside India for an invention based on
 research or information pertaining to a biological resource obtained from India.
(b) State Biodiversity Boards will deal with matters relating to access by Indians for
 commercial purposes and restrict any activity which violates the objectives of
 conservation, sustainable use and equitable sharing of benefits.
(c) Biodiversity Management Committees will be set up by institutions of self-
government in their respective areas for conservation, sustainable use,
 documentation of biodiversity and chronicling of knowledge relating to
 biodiversity. Biodiversity Management Committees shall be consulted by the
 National Biodiversity Authority and State Biodiversity Boards on matters related to
 use of biological resources and associated knowledge within their jurisdiction

 expenses and contingency etc, will be of the order of Rs. 80 lakhs per annum. Non-recurring
 expenditure on establishment, office equipment, vehicles, etc. will be approximately of the order
 of Rs. 50 lakhs.
MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION
Clause 60 of the Bill empowers the Central Government to make rules by notification in the
 official Gazette for carrying out the purposes of the proposed legislation. Sub-clause (2) of that
 clause enumerates the matters with respect to which rules may be made under the proposed
 legislation. These matters inter-alia relate to the terms of office; the salary and allowances and
 conditions of the Chairperson and members of the National Biodiversity Authority; powers and
 duties of Chairperson, transaction of business of the National Biodiversity Authority, form of
 application and payment of fees for undertaking certain activities; the procedure for adjudication,
 etc.
2. Clause 61 of the Bill empowers the State Governments to make rules by notification in the
 official Gazette for carrying out purposes of this proposed legislation. Sub-clause (2) of that
 clause enumerates the various matters with respect to which rules may be made under this
 legislation. These matters inter alia relate to the form in which the prior intimation shall be given;
 rules for the management and conservation of heritage sites; management of the Local
 Biodiversity Fund, etc.
3. Clause 62 of the Bill empowers the National Biodiversity Authority to make regulations with
 the previous approval of the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette.
4. The rules and regulations made under the proposed legislation shall be required to be laid
 before Parliament.
5. The aforesaid matters in respect of which rules, regulations may be made or framed relate to
 matters of procedure or administrative detail and it is not practicable to provide for them in the
 Bill itself. The delegation of legislative power is, therefore of a normal character.

Action Taken by the Department
Necessity for the Programme:
The necessity for undertaking the Himalayan Glaciology Programme has been felt by DST because the study of Himalayan
 Glaciers is important and significant due to the following factors:
(a)  Glaciers & snow fields are an important source of fresh water and their melt water support the flow of Indus, Ganga and
 Brahmaputra rivers and their tributaries. It is important to know the behaviour of glaciers for planning hydroelectric
 power projects, roads, and other utility services of national importance such as floods/avalanche monitoring and
 management. Glacier studies are being carried out all over the world for similar purposes.
(b) The climate and weather pattern of India is greatly influenced by Himalaya and Himalayan glaciers and snow fields.
 Glacier fluctuation has been identified as one of the Geo-indicators useful to assess the geological aspect of global
 climate change.  It was identified in Agenda 21 of the 1992 United Nations Rio Conference on the Environment.    
 Therefore, no country in the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra river basins can afford to ignore the glaciers.
(c)  Glacier advance or recession is an important environmental parameter. Glaciers are sensitive barometers of climate
 change, growing and dwarfing in response to the changes in temperature and snowfall. So, the glacier fluctuations of
 past and present  serve as valuable source of  information for regional and global climate, melt water flow,
 environmental change in mountain region and their adjoining   plains. Being intimately connected with various
 geological processes, glaciers provide insight into the geology of Himalayas.
(d)  The valley glaciers and other related formations are part of the geomorphic pattern of the Himalaya.
DST’s Enthusiasm and Zeal for the Programme:
DST is coordinating/promoting studies on Himalayan Glaciers as also providing financial assistance for research and
 development activities so as to generate a strong R&D database for future studies  on the  subject.  DST has been  playing a
 pivotal  role to  provide a platform for  its
 sister organizations and academic/research institutions for pursuing research in
 identified priority areas and undertaking coordinated multi- institutional and multi-disciplinary research activities in selected
 major glaciers of national importance.  DST is very much keen to make all out effort to chalk out strategies so as to
 stimulate/encourage scientists and creating scientific temper which in turn may strengthen the Himalayan Glaciology
 programme.
Some of the important activities to be implemented by DST in the near future are as follows:-
In addition to on-going activities, DST has proposed a multidisciplinary and multi-institutional coordinated project to study
 the Dokriani Bamak Glacier. The project is now under consideration of DST funding. There are 8 research institutions involved
 in this project to study various aspects of the Dokriani Bamak Glacier.
DST has also proposed collaboration at international level to take joint studies and training of manpower. The proposal is
 being taken up by the International Division of DST with other Central Asian Region countries. ,
A project on "National Snow Science Workshop" to be organized by SASE, Chandigarh, is also under consideration of DST
 funding. The workshop will provide an opportunity to the scientists of the country to express their views and come out with
 future strategies in the field of glaciology.
As in the past, the emphasis will be laid on manpower development. Geological Survey of India (GSI) has trained a number
 of scientists in last five years involving DST support. Efforts will be made to organize field-oriented training programme for the
 promising young scientists who then could take up research activities.
Glaciological research has been pursued for long in the country with different levels of success. These studies were more or
 less carried out with limited objectives. Now, it has become very clear that the science of glaciology should be pursued in the
 country by a totally dedicated Centre. With this aim, a proposal to set up a National Centre for Field Operations and Research
 on Himalayan Glaciology (NCFOR-HG) has been prepared. The National Centre would strive to generate a strong in-house
 research base as well as a network of state-of-the-art laboratories mid field operation facilities which will also be available to
 researchers from other centers and Universities across the country for their investigations. The National Centre will bring
 holistic approach to the Himalayan glaciological research in the country and provide much needed data base for formulation of
 national policies on natural resource management in glacier regions of the country.
Efforts are on to disseminate information and to popularize the programme widely among scientists of the country. To
 achieve this target, a Brochure on Himalayan Glaciology is likely to come out shortly. A website on the programme is also
 being -planned to be accessed through INTERNET. Similarly, periodical publication of a News Letter on Himalayan
 Glaciology is under consideration.

R E P O R T
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Ocean Development on the
 recommendations contained in the Eighty-eight Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of the Department of Ocean
 Development which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 20th April, 2001 and laid on the table of Lok Sabha on the 20 th
 April, 2001.  There are eighteen recommendations contained in the eighty-eight Report of the Committee. Action Taken
 notes on the recommendations of the Committee were received from the Department on 23rd October, 2001.
The Committee’s recommendations, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the action taken by the
 Department of Ocean Development are set out in the succeeding paragraphs: -
BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS FOR 2001-02
Recommendation 
The Committee observes that in view of considerable reduction in the Budgetary support at RE level last year, it
 should be possible for the Department to manage with the reduced budgetary support this year.  To that end the
 Committee brings on record the assurance given by the Department in reply to Question 1 of the Questionnaire (See
 Appendix) that the present outlay will not hold up the execution of any programme.
                                                                                                                                  (Para 14)
Action Taken by the Department
The Department is grateful for the concern shown by the Committee with regard to the reduction in the budgetary
 support for the current year.  The Department would like to re-assure the Committee that the present outlay will not hold up
 the execution of any programme.
Comments:
The Committee notes the reply.
Recommendation
In the context of delay in the Commissioning the Technology Demonstration Pilot Plant for extraction of metals
 from Poly Metallic Nodules at Hindustan Zinc Ltd., at Udaipur, HZL (U), which  was to be commissioned in
 October, 2000 and the Pilot Plant which was expected to be commissioned off Tuticorin coast in September-October,
 2000, the Committee observes that such delays result in cost escalations.  Besides, they reflect on the Departments’
 efficiency to plan things meticulously.  Such delays need to be avoided.
                                                                                                            (Para 15)
Action Taken by the Department
It is submitted that the initiation of the project was delayed for few months due to delay in the finalization of the contract
 for the erection & commissioning of the plant by HZL (U). The plant is now scheduled for commissioning in October, 2001
 without any cost escalation.
As regards the commissioning of the floating OTEC Plant off Tuticorin, there were delays in completing the two main
 components viz., the plant barge and the sea water system. These delays were due to delayed supply by vendors and some
 teething problem during fabrication.  Finally, however, when the sea water systems were being deployed there was a mishap
 resulting in loss of the pipelines. This has caused a set back to the project which is now expected to be commissioned only
 by mid 2002.  The Committee’s directions have been noted and every effort would be made to ensure completion of projects
 as per schedule.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply and hopes that steps would be taken to ensure such delays do not reoccur and

 timely completion of projects is carried out.  The Committee would also like to know whether cost escalation would
 take place in commissioning of the floating OTEC Plant off Tuticorin if commissioned by mid of 2002 and how it will

Recommendation
As regards the reasons advanced for non-utilisation of the budgetary support in respect of continental shelf and
 Poly Metallic Nodules programme, the Committee is concernd with the delays in finalizing the contracts and
 observes such delays could have been avoided.
(Para 17)
Action Taken by the Department
In relation to continental shelf programme the delay in finalizing the contract was on account of
(i)
                  new understanding about the geology of Laxmi Basin in Arabian Sea and thereby changing the technical
 parameters of the tender as per the provisions of Scientific and Technical Guidelines of the Commission and
(ii)                delay in initiating the discussion with Sri Lanka which are crucial in implementing the provisions of Law of
 the Sea.
While the technical parameters for the tender are under the final stages of confirmation, Ministry of External Affairs is
 taking up the matter with Sri Lanka, which is critical for undertaking survey.
Comments
The Committee feels that the Department should pursue with Ministry of External affairs for taking up the
 matter with the Sri Lankan government to reach an agreement so that any delay on this account is minimized.

Recommendation
As regards the difficulties being faced by the Department on the non-plan side with regard to the payments to the
 Shipping Corporation of India for the operation of the Research Vessels “Sagar Kanya” and Sagar Sampada”, while the
 committee is all out for reduction of non-plan expenditure, but in view of the seriousness of the expenditure for Research
 Vessels, the Committee feels that it is a kind of committed expenditure and the Department should not be compelled to
 dither on its commitments, the Committee recommends that the budgetary support on this count be suitably augmented now
 or at least at RE stage or else the research vessels may remain idle and consequently the research effort may suffer which
 would not be healthy development.                                                                                                                            (Para 19)
Action Taken by the Department
The non-plan BE 2001-02 for FORV Sagar Sampada is Rs. 10.31 crore.  Taking into consideration the mandatory need
 for dry dock repairs of the vessel during 2001-02 and the critical need to upgrade the scientific facilities on board, the BE
 under FORV non-plan head 2001-02 need to be enhanced by at least Rs. 1 crore at the RE stage.  The non-plan BE 2001-02
 for ORV Sagar Kanya is Rs. 13.12 crore.   
Comments
The Committee observes that the Department should have indicated the action taken for augmenting the budgetary
 requirements.  The Department should now take up the matter with the Ministries/Departments concerned for suitably
 augmenting the budgetary support.

The Committee feels that the baseline data collected by National Hydrographic Office (NHO) should be analysed in
 consultation with National Institutions like Geological Survey of India, National Institute of Oceanography, National
 Geophysical Research Institute etc., for estimating the foot of the slope and 2500 m isobath in accordance with the format
 specified in the guidelines of the Commission.

Action Taken by the Department

The Committee observes that under Marine Living Resources programme the Department of Ocean Development should
 emphasize on the coverage of entire Indian Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) for the Winter, Summer and Inter Monsoon

 area.

The programme was originally proposed to cover the entire Indian Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ).  However, since the
 programme is based on observations/data collection from only a single vessel, i.e. FORV Sagar Sampada, coverage of some 
 of the stations could  not  be done  for all the seasons Centre for Marine Living Resources (CMLRE) has already  proposed 
 to fill  the gaps by continuing the programme in the 10
th Plan where a provision for hiring of an additional vessel has also
 been projected.
CMLRE has taken up a new project on use of Hydro-acoustics for Deep Scattering Layer (DSL) and fish Biomass

 Estimation and the work has just been commenced.
Project proposal with regard to “Column Productivity” and “Inventorying of Marine Bioresources of continental slope
 area”, has already been finalized and are proposed to be taken up during 10th Plan.
Comments:
The Committee notes the position.
DRUGS FROM SEA
Recommendation
The Committee observes that the programme regarding development of six marine organisms showing anti-
diabetic/antidiarrahoeal; anti-hyperlipidaelmic, anti-anxiety, anti-cholesterol cum anti-oxidant; anti-bacterial cum anti-fungal
 and larvicidal activities is more or less at the same stage as was at the last year with no signs of the end product coming to
 market in the near future.  In these circumstances the Committee does not find any justification in the new projects on herbal
 drugs being undertaken.  Unless the drugs are developed expeditiously and brought into markets, the market forces could
 defeat the purpose of developing the drugs and render the whole project infructuous and futile.
                                     (Para 34)
Action Taken by the Department
Out of the organisms identified for anti-diabetic, anti-diarrhoeal, anti-hyperlipidaemic, anti-anxiety, anti-cholesterol cum
 anti-oxidant, anti-bacterial cum anti-fungal and larvicidal activities, substantial progress has been made in the development
 of marine organisms identified for anti-diabetic, anti-diarrhoeal and anti-hyperlipidaemic activities besides continuing with
 the ongoing exploratory activity.  Their activities have been revalidated in repeat collection and regulatory sub-acute
 toxicity studies in two rodent species. The organisms have been found to be safe and devoid of any side effect.  The
 regulatory sub-acute toxicity studies in primates are in progress and are likely to be completed by the end of 2001.
The regulatory  pharmacological studies have also clearly indicated that anti-diabetic, anti-diarrhoeal and anti-
hyperlipidaemic preparations are devoid of any other physiological effects.  After toxicity studies in monkeys tie-up with
 pharmaceutical will be explored in the early part of 2002.  The clinical trials are expected to be initiated after obtaining the
 statutory permissions of the Drugs Controller General of India sometime in 2002.
It may also be pointed out that 13 organisms have further been identified for various therapeutic activities and work on
 them is being done vigorously.  It is expected that out of these 3-4 molecules will be identified for further development of
 potential drugs in future.
Comments
While the Committee notes the reply, it would like to impress on the Department the need to develop and market the end
 product at the earliest without circumventing the process/procedures or prescribed legal requirements.
MARINE NON-LIVING RESOURCES
Poly Metallic Nodules Programme
Recommendation
The Committee observes that the Poly Metallic Nodules Programme commenced in 1987.  The Department claims to
 have made considerable progress for exploration and exploitation of Poly Metallic Nodules ever since the country attained
 this status in the field of survey and exploration.  While a proposal for developing an unmanned submersible capable of
 operation upto 6000 m depth has been approved for which NIOT has been identified as the nodal agency, so far we have
 only been able to achieve upgraded version of ROV developed by Central Mechanical Engineering Research Institute,
 Durgapur which is ready for a test in open sea up to a depth of 250 m only.  Besides, a test for a sampling of slurry through a
 rise hose from 410 m water depth were done earlier.  If the depths of 250 to 410 m are any indication it would be a long
 journey to reach the test level of 6000 m.

Observation is noted.
Comments
The Committee observes that the Department should continue its efforts to reach the desired level of achievement which

 how & Transfer of technology.

The Department is also of the view (please see reply to Question 4 in the Questionnaire at Annexure) that current state of

Action Taken by the Department
The Department has constituted a “Group of Experts” on 27.8.2001.  The Group of Experts shall assess the viability of
 the programme in view of fast changing technologies considering long gestation, cost of production and economics of

Comments
The Committee was apprised earlier that Polymetallic Nodule Programme was in experimental stage.  Therefore, the
 commercial exploitation of the project/Programme would not be feasible for some more time. 
The Committee was also apprised at the time of consideration of Demands for Grants of the Department for the year

Attention is also invited to the observation of the Committee contained in the Sixty-fifth (paragraph 25) and Eighty-
eighth reports of the Department aforesaid the Committee observes that it is doubtful whether the programmes requiring

COASTAL RESEARCH VESSELS  (CRV)
Recommendation
While the Committee has made its observation about the Committed liabilities towards the Shipping Corporation of
 India, the Committee would like the Department to assess whether it was time to go in for any new ships of this kind
 keeping in view the state of its requirements, the life span left for both the ships, costs involved in acquiring new ships and

                                                                                                                              (Para 44)
Action Taken by the Department
FORV Sagar Sampada commissioned in 1984 is already 17 years old.  With proper maintenance, it is likely to be
 operational for another 8 years.  To facilitate this, it is essential to undertake overhauling of the vessel during 2002-2003,
 which include major repair/replacement works on the hydraulic system, winches, Evac system, vessel engine, strengthening
 the deck-plates and floor of cabins, installing stabilizer fence, augmenting accommodation facilities etc. An approximate
 expenditure of Rs. 4 crore is anticipated.
Considering the requirements to meet the objectives of the Marine Living Resources programme including survey of the
 Southern Ocean resources, it is essential to have a minimum of 2 dedicated Fishery Oceanography Research Vessels. 
 During the 10
th plan period, the requirements are proposed to be met by chartering one research vessel for 100 day/year for
 which separate budgetary provisions are incorporated in the proposal submitted by Centre for Marine Living Resources
 (CMLRE).
The lead time required for the planning, designing, building and commissioning of a new ice-class Research vessel will
 be approximately 5 years.  In view of this, it is necessary to initiate actions during the 10 th plan period itself, so that such a
 vessel is available by the year 2008.  The requirements of the new vessel, as identified by a Departmental Committee which
 met at Kochi on 7th & 8th of April, 2000, should include facilities for long-line, squid jigging etc; and should be designed to

 will be around Rs. 200 crores.
The Steering Committee for the formulation of X Five year plan has set up a Working Group for the Department of
 Ocean Development under the Chairmanship of the Secretary DOD.  The Working Group further constituted Group of
 Experts committees on each of the major areas. One of such areas was “New Research Vessel” under the Chairmanship of
 Prof. B.L.K. Somayajulu.  The Experts Committee met to discuss the state of existing research vessels available with the
 DOD, CSIR, GSI, CIFT and FSI.  The capabilities of the existing vessels, their life span, up-gradations have been examined
 in the light of the research programmes envisaged on living and non-living resources during the X plan.  The committee

NEW DELHI;                                                                                                                 C. RAMACHANDRAIAH,
March 20, 2002                                                                                                                            Chairman,

R E P O R T
 
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Environment & Forests on the
 recommendations contained in the Ninetieth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Science & Technology, Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2001-2002) of the Ministry of Environment
 & Forests which was presented to the Rajya Sabha on 24 th  April, 2001 and laid in the Lok Sabha on the 24 th April,
 2001.  There are 20 recommendations contained in the Ninetieth Report of the Committee. Action Taken notes on the
 recommendations of the Committee were received from the Department on 15th October, 2001.
The Committee’s recommendations, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee on the action taken by the
 Ministry of Environment & Forests are set out in the succeeding paragraphs: -
MAJOR SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY
Recommendation 
The Committee observes that there is need for radical transformation in the attitude of officials concerned with
 inspection of the level of pollution generated by industrial units. The attitude should be objective, need based and be
 guided by the need to control the pollution in the interest of present generation as well as posterity.
The Ministry should also prepare an Action Plan for already identified 24 critically polluted areas of the country for
 improvement of Environment.
(Para 8.2)
Action Taken by the Department
The observations of the Committee have been noted and would be conveyed to Central Pollution Control Board/State
 Pollution Control Boards for its implementation.
The Central Pollution Control Board in consultation with the State Pollution Control Boards has prepared Action
 Plan for the 24 critically polluted areas which is under implementation.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
VEHICULAR POLLUTION CONTROL MEASURES
Recommendation
The Committee observes that the national emission standards introduced by the Government are nothing more than
 the minimum requirement. In the interest of a clean environment there is perhaps a need for more rigid standards. At the

file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/98th.htm[29-08-2018 16:20:38]
 same time there is a need to consider whether any particular type of fuel or gas, say CNG alone will result in a clean and
 green environment. Whether it is safe to use it? A decision has to be taken, keeping in view the infrastructure available
 and without causing hardships to commuters and throwing the entire economy out of gear.
The Committee is aware that the Ministry of Environment & Forests enjoys statutory powers under the Air
 Act, 1981 and the Environment (Protection) Act to enforce more stringent regime of standards with a view to 
 control  pollution.  The Ministry  should  have stepped in  the  current controversy with regard to use of CNG in
 public transport and help bring a harmonious solution to the problem with a view to control the pollution
 without causing hardships to any section of the society.
(Para 9.1 and 9.2 )
Action Taken by the Department
An inter-ministerial Task Force on Auto Fuels Specifications and Vehicular Emission Standards constituted under
 the Chairmanship of Chairman, Central Pollution Control Board submitted its report in March, 2001 to the Ministry of
 Petroleum and Natural Gas. The report includes the following recommendations: -
" From the environmental angle and for reduction in vehicular emissions, an ideal option would have been to achieve
 Euro-IV standards from the year 2005 which will bring us at par with the European Union norms. However, in view of
 the fact that the Euro-IV specifications and technologies are yet to be firmed up, and that taking a jump from Bharat
 Stage I norms akin to Euro I norms to Euro III norms in the entire country may not be implement able, the suggested
 option will be to achieve Bharat Stage II norms throughout the country by 2005 and to strive for achieving Euro-III
 equivalent (Bharat Stage III) norms from the year 2005 in mega cities (NCT/NCR, Greater Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai,
 Bangalore, Hyderabad & Ahmedabad)."
As regards to use of CNG as a transport fuel with special reference to public transport in the NCR, the Hon'ble
 Supreme Court has given directions vide its order dated 28
th  July, 1998 which include the following:
Expansion of CNG outlets from 9 to 80 by 31.03.2000.
Replacement of all pre 1990 autos and taxis with new vehicles using clean fuel.
Entire city bus fleet (DTC & Private) to be converted to single fuel mode on CNG by       31.03.2001.
These orders are being implemented. CNG is a clean fuel and overall CNG vehicles are safer than other vehicles.
 The risk as a result of fire or as a result of uncontrolled release of CNG is much lower than gasoline and comparable to
 that which might be expected with diesel fuel. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways is dealing the matter
 relating to adoption of safety code of practice for CNG vehicles under the Central Motor Vehicle Rules. The Ministry of
 Environment and Forests is regularly coordinating with the concerned agencies including Government of NCT of Delhi,
 the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas to bring harmonious
 solution to use CNG in public transport with a view to control air pollution in Delhi.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
NATIONAL RIVER CONSERVATION PLAN INCLUDING GANGA ACTION PLAN
Recommendation
The Committee observes that for any plan or programme regarding cleansing of rivers of such a magnitude as
 Ganga, to succeed, it is necessary to have a meticulous planning. Any delay in its execution is bound to result in
 the plan going awry. More so, because the parameters regarding the  size of the  population and  the extent of
 urbanisation etc., which
 would have been taken into account at the stage of planning are subject to rapid changes
 in a country like India. Hence, timely execution is crucial for such programmes or else we would be back to
 square one.
(Para 10.2)
Action Taken by the Department
The Ministry acknowledges the need for timely execution of the programme. The following steps have been taken by
 the Ministry to speed up the progress of implementation-

file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/98th.htm[29-08-2018 16:20:38]
(i)   A Standing Committee of NRCA has been constituted under the Union Minister of Environment & Forests to
 enable a more frequent review of the progress of the programme.
(ii)  The programme is reviewed at regular intervals by the Monitoring Committee chaired by Member
 (Environment), Planning Commission and the Steering Committee chaired by Secretary, Ministry of
 Environment & Forests.
(iii)The Chief Ministers of the Ganga Action Plan (GAP) States have been requested to constitute review
 Committees under them with MPs, MLAs, Mayor of local bodies to review the progress of the programme on
 regular basis.
(iv)The Nodal Secretaries of various State Departments have been asked to review the programme with their
 respective implementation agencies on a regular basis.
(v)  Site visits are regularly undertaken by the NRCD officers to review and monitor the progress of works.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry and observes that the Central Ganga Authority now National
 River Conservation Authority had time and again emphasized that the project under Ganga Action Plan should
 be implemented in a time bound manner and the steps mentioned above were already in place.  But even after a
 period of 10 years, the GAP- Phase I is not fully complete and the time schedule for GAP- Phase II i.e. December
 2001 has lapsed and only 13.7 percent of the targeted sewage treatment capacity has been created.  It is a sad
 state of affairs.  The Committee would like the Ministry to take steps for speedy execution of the Plan.
Recommendation
At the same time it is necessary to see whether any alternative effective indigenous technologies can be
 advantageously used instead of draining out vast sums from national exchequer for which no audit may be possible.
(Para 10.3)
Action Taken by the Department
Keeping in view the experience gained under GAP Phase-1, emphasis is being placed by NRCD for promoting
 appropriate and low cost technologies for treatment of sewage, which also have lower O&M costs. Thus, where
 adequate land is available, technologies like waste stabilisation ponds, agro-forestry (Karnal) are being preferred. The
 State Governments have been asked to carry out the life cycle cost comparison of various technologies (which includes
 capital cost, land cost and O&M cost) before determining the most optimum technology for a particular site.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
RECEOMMENDATION OF THE COMMITTEE
The Committee has been given to understand that a team of experts from Varanasi has devised a method to rid the
 Ganga of a big chunk of its pollutant load, using the inherent energy of the flowing waters and the sun and the filtering
 properties of the riverbed.
Banaras Hindu University's (BHU) Ganga Laboratory has developed the "three gradient theory", using the
 river's sand bed, solar energy and the kinetic energy of the water that could prove a vital pollution management
 tool in cities located along the country's rivers that are struggling to contain water pollution.
The Committee understands that the system basically filters the inorganic, organic and microbiological pollutant load
 of the river - usually left untreated by sewage treatment plants (STPS) - through the sand piled up on the concave bank
 or downstream and upstream of the city.
"The polluted water first flows out of a trickling box - which is large filter comprising sand and stone layers and then
 the sand bed. If then mingles with the high velocity zone in the river for a natural course of flow again". The problem of
 pollution is acute between December and July, which is the dry season, when the river level falls below 65 meters and
 the dissolved oxygen also decreases. But this energizes the sand bed as solar radiation converts it into a hot plate to treat
 a higher quantum of inorganic and microbiological waste.
(Para 10.4 to 10.7) 

file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/98th.htm[29-08-2018 16:20:38]
Action Taken by the Department
Prof U. K. Choudhary of Department of Civil Engineering, BHU, Varanasi submitted a project proposal in April,
 1995 suggesting application of five theories of Science & Technology and the theory of Three Gradients for river
 pollution management without treatment plants and power supply for pollution abatement of river Ganga at Varanasi
 under Ganga Action Plan  Phase-II. According to the proposal, the sewage generated in Varanasi city is to be taken to
 the opposite side of the river Ganga by pumping and symphonic pipe arrangement and sprinkled over the sand bed
 which will act as a trickling filter and treat the sewage. The treated effluent from the sand bed will rejoin the river.
The proposal of Prof. U.K. Choudhary was referred to Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and U.P.
 Government in May/June, 1995 for their examination and expert advice. Both the U.P. Government and Central
 Pollution Control Board rejected the proposal of Prof. U.K. Choudhary as very expensive, impractical and technically
 not feasible due to the following reasons:
(i)   It is impractical and expensive to take the wastewater to the opposite side of the river at Varanasi by laying
 pipelines below the bed of the river, the width of which is a few kilometers particularly in the rainy season. 
(ii)  There is every possibility of chokage of pores of the sand bed due to entrainment of suspended solids present in
 the sewage. This will cause the proposed trickling filter to choke after sometime, as a result of which the sewage
 and pathogens instead of going through the filter media would go into the river as surface flow without any
 treatment, thereby, polluting it.
(iii)The RL of the proposed treatment site is 64 meters, whereas the normal flood level of river Ganga in Varanasi is
 71 meters. The proposed treatment plant site which falls in the flood plain of river Ganga would be submerged in
 flood water every year for 30-45 days in the monsoon season. Construction of sewage treatment plant the flood
 plain of the river should be avoided as a basic concept.
(iv)Since both banks of river Ganga are used for bathing by the pilgrims on festive occasions, carrying the waste
 water to the opposite bank will pollute the environment on that side. Thus, there is a risk of health hazard and
 discomfort to the pilgrims during the mass bathing days.
3.   In November 1995, NRCD informed Prof. U.K.Choudhary that his proposal was not acceptable in view of the
 comments/advice received from Central Pollution Control Board and UP Government.

Recommendation
The Committee observes that Ganga Action plan, launched in 1985, with the objective of bringing water
 quality of river Ganga and its tributaries to bathing levels, has not been able to achieve its objective till date.
 GAP Phase-I of the plan is not yet fully complete, even after delay of over 10 years. GAP Phase-II is also far
 behind schedule, and is due to end in December, 2001. There are reports of creation of only 13.7% of the targeted
 sewage treatment capacity so far. The assets created under the Scheme suffered serious impairment and often
 closure particularly in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh because of technical flaws in design, problems in land
 acquisition, contract mismanagement, lack of maintenance and in general because of the lackadaisical attitude of
 the States and their implementing agencies.  Technologies adopted by the National River Conservation
 Directorate (NRCD) for construction of Sewage Treatment Plants (STPS) were often questionable in as much as
 they could not adequately address the problem of reducing bacterial load in the river to the desired level. The
 NRCD has abandoned the crucial activity of monitoring the water quality on river Ganga since September, 1999,
 reportedly for want of funds, and deprived itself of a key instrument of overall performance monitoring of the
 GAP. The Ministry of Environment & Forests needs to seriously review the implementing of entire GAP and
 evolve a financing arrangements whereby the States and the agencies develop a more involved stake in
 arrangement whereby the States and the agencies develop a more involved stake in creation of assets, their
 maintenance and their functionality at all times; review and strengthen technical and administrative monitoring
 to ensure the value for money and  assets created at great public expense; and facilitate competent technological

 support for optimum utilization of resources.
(Para 10.10)
Action Taken by the Department
The GAP was launched in 1985 with the objective of bringing water quality of river Ganga and its tributaries to
 bathing levels. The total expenditure on the scheme till March 31, 2000 is Rs. 903.88 crore and till November 30, 2000
 is Rs. 930.79 crore. The Ganga Action Plan (GAP) referred to in the CAG report includes works under GAP -Phase I
 and II. The scheme GAP-1, which was started in 1985, has been declared closed on 31.3.2000 although 3 sub-schemes
 of sewage treatment plants are yet to be completed (2 in Bihar and 1 in West Bengal). The total expenditure on this Plan
 is Rs. 452 crore. Pollution abatement works in 25 towns in the States of UP, Bihar, and West Bengal have been taken up
 under GAP Phase 1. Under this Plan, a capacity of 835 mld has been created against the target of 873 mld. The
 estimated sewage in 25 towns in 1985 was 1340 mld. Thus, pollution load treated in terms of pollution level of 1985 is
 about 65% but in terms of present pollution level, it will amount to 35% only. Certain problems of O&M of assets
 created under GAP-1 have emerged in Bihar and to some extent in UP. The matter is being constantly pursued with the
 State Government at the highest level. It is also proposed to move the Planning Commission to consider earmarking of
 O&M Funds in the State Annual Plans. These are the major reasons for low visibility of impact of GAP-1 on the water
 quality of river Ganga. However, the water quality monitoring results indicate that wherever the Pollution abatement
 works have been commissioned and made functional, the river water quality has shown improvement for  example, in 
 1986 the  bio chemical  oxygen demand (BOD) ranged from 5.5 to 15.5 mg/lt in the stretch from Kannouj to Varanasi as
 against which, the values of BOD in this stretch ranged from 1.8 to 6.5 mg/l in 1999.
2.   As for the GAP-II, this Programme was approved in 3 phases from 1993 to 1996. GAP-II was later merged under the
 National River Conservation Plan (NRCP) in December 1996. A total capacity of about 1861 mld of sewage treatment
 alongwith allied works is to be created under GAP-II. The works of YAP under GAP-II in Haryana (12 towns), UP (8
 towns) and Delhi are in an advanced stage of completion. As against the present approved cost of Rs. 509 crore an
 expenditure of Rs. 453 crore has been incurred on the Plan so far. The targeted sewage treatment capacity of 744 mld, in
 the original 15 towns (Haryana-6, U.P.-S and Delhi) which is funded by the Japan Bank for International Cooperation
 (JBIC) through a soft loan has been commissioned and made functional. The remaining about 78 mld capacity at Agra is
 also under commissioning. The works in the remaining 6 towns of Haryana under YAP will take another 2 years to
 complete. The works on the other components of GAP-II which cover the river Ganga, Gomati and Damodar are in
 different stages of execution. The objective of the scheme can be expected to be achieved only when all the ongoing
 works under GAP-II are completed.
3.   Out of the total of 5414 mld of domestic sewage in 109 towns selected for pollution abatement along the banks of
 river Ganga and its tributaries, the GAP addressed to process only 2734 mld. The remaining quantity of 2680 mld is for
 Delhi which is being tackled with their own Plan funds. As against the target of 2734 mld under GAP the total capacity
 of sewage treatment created under Ganga Action Plan -I and II till date is 1559 mld which is 57 per cent of the target.
4.  The conventional technologies proposed earlier did not address the problems of bacterial pollution fully. In order to
 address this issue, a decision was taken in July 1999 to adopt oxidation pond based sewage treatment in all the places.
 These ponds although requiring large areas of land are capable of reducing faucal coliform suitably. The State
 Governments could not provide such areas of land in large towns, which account for a major chunk of the capital cost of
 works under the Action Plan. In view of the difficulties of land acquisition in large towns it has now been decided to use
 conventional system of sewage treatment followed by dis-infection to address the bacteriological pollution.
5.  The discontinuation of water quality monitoring was done considering the fact that under the ongoing
 GEMS/MINARS programmes of CPCB, the water quality of major river is being monitored with the help of SPCBs and
 the data generated there could be utilised. However, it was observed that the water quality monitoring of CPCBs does
 not meet the objective of GAP and the submission of data is late. The Water Quality Monitoring (WQM) under GAP
 was restarted from December 2000.
6.   A comprehensive monitoring mechanism at the Centre and in the States is in place for Ganga Action Plan. The
 programme is monitored by an Apex Committee called the National River Conservation Authority (NRCA) (earlier
 called the Central Ganga Authority) which is chaired by the Prime Minister and has the Union Minister of Environment
 and Forests and other Central Ministers of the concerned Ministries, Chief Ministers and Members of Parliament of the
 participating States as Members. So far, 10 meetings of NRCA have been held. The last meeting was held on 13. 3.
 2001. There is a Steering Committee under Secretary of the Ministry of Environment and Forests with the Chief

 Secretary of the participating States and officers of the concerned Central Ministries as Members. The Steering
 Committee reviews the programme on a quarterly basis. Till date a total of 45 meetings have been held. In addition a
 Monitoring Committee under the Chairmanship of Member Planning Commission also reviews progress on a quarterly
 basis. A total of 30 (as on 31.3.2001) meetings of the Monitoring Committee have been held so far. In addition to these
 Committees, the progress both physical and financial is regularly reviewed by the Ministry for Environment and Forests
 with the concerned officers of the State Government. The NRCD, which is implementing this programme, has regular

 nodal implementing agency earmarked for this programme. The Secretary of Nodal Department reviews the progress on
 a regular basis. Additionally, there is a Steering Committee which reviews the programme on a quarterly basis. The
 Citizens Monitoring Committees have also been constituted in most of the GAP towns to review the progress and
 provide inputs for public participation and involvement.
7.   In the 10
th  Meeting of NRCA held on 13.3.2001 under the Chairmanship of Prime Minister, a total of 11 resolutions
 were adopted as given in Annexure. With the integration and holistic approach and with direct public participation in the
 cost as proposed in these resolutions, the programme is expected to achieve the much-desired sustainability. The
 Ministry of Environment and Forests is also moving the Planning Commission for earmarking funds for O&M out of
 the State Annual Plans.

The Committee observes that Rs.453 crore has been incurred on the Plan so far as against the present approved

WILD LIFE PROTECTION
Recommendation
 The Committee is constrained to observe that despite the Wild Life Protection Act, 1972 and other enactments, there
 has been a spurt in death of animals in recent years, like Rhinos, tigers, elephants, peacocks etc. in one or other parts of
 the country. Besides, there have been cases of poaching and smuggling of Wild-Life specially the Tigers on the Indo-
Nepal Boarder. The Committee observes that the steps taken by the Government at State, National and international
 level are mere reiteration of what already exists in the statue book or elsewhere.
(Para 15)
Action Taken by the Department
There is no denying the fact that there has been rise in the number of seizures of wildlife products/deaths of animals
 like rhinos, tigers, elephants, peacocks over the years. This is also a fact  that  large number of cases of poaching of
 tigers have been detected in Lakhimpur Kheri and other Tarai districts of Uttar Pradesh. increase in the number of
 offences is partly also due to better detection both on account of greater sensitization of enforcement agencies as well as
 the authorization of new expert investigative agencies like the CBI and Special Task Forces of State Police Departments
 to investigate the cases of violation of Wild Life (Protection) Act.
The monetary incentive for poaching and clandestine trade in wildlife has become so lucrative that highly organised
 mafias have entered into this field. Most of the times the kingpin of the Organisation conducts the operations sitting at a
 distance and the enforcement agencies end up by arresting persons who do not have much information about the final
 destination of the products  and  the  principal  beneficiary  of  the  operation.  Lack  of  investigation skills with the
 enforcement agencies and the slow process of prosecution in the courts further compound the problem.
These issues were discussed at length in the meeting of the State Minister of Forests held at Coimbatore in January,
 200 1. The main recommendations in the Charter are :
1.  Wild animals do considerable damage to agricultural crops in areas adjoining national parks and sanctuaries,
 causing considerable concern, thereby requiring formulation of an appropriate insurance scheme for
 compensating damage to agricultural crops failing within five kilometers of national parks and sanctuaries.

4.   An effective mechanism for intelligence gathering and data base of habitual offenders should be developed for
 preventing wildlife crimes.
5. Adequate expertise shall be developed for prosecuting offenders and training be organised for undertaking

6.   Steps shall be taken immediately for designating special courts for wildlife offences.
7.  Create effective enforcement infrastructure both within protected areas and outside protected area to prevent

It was followed up by a comprehensive message from the Prime Minister of India, copy of which is annexed.

ANNEXURES
 
  ANNEXURE - I
RESOLUTIONS ADOPTED AT THE X MEETING OF THE NRCA HELD ON 13.3.2001
 The X meeting of the National River Conservation Authority (NRCA) was held on 13.3.2001 at 5.00 PM in the
 Parliament House Annexe under the Chairmanship of Hon'ble Prime Minister. The meeting was attended by Union
 Minister for Environment & Forests, Dy. Chairman, Planning Commission, Member Planning Commission, Members
 of Parliament, Chief Ministers of four States, Environment Ministers and senior officials of States and senior officials of
 various Ministries of Central Government. NRCA after detailed deliberation unanimously adopted following resolution:
1.   While river cleaning would need to be given a much higher priority, it is also essential that resources are not
 spread thinly. The focus, therefore, has to be on large towns, which are gross polluters.
2.   In case of works already completed assets need to be maintained and also continuously operated/utilized for
 which funds must be earmarked by the States. The State& UTs must meet the O&M costs which on an average
 is around 5% of the capital cost.
3.   A holistic and integrated approach shall be adopted by addressing not only river pollution but other components
 like internal sewage, solid waster disposal, low cost toilets etc.
4.   The cost of works shall be shared between the Central and States/local bodies, public on 70:30 basis. The public
 shall contribute not less than 10% of the cost.
5.   A detailed plan for recovery/operation maintenance cost shall become part of the project proposal in future,
6.   Because of delay in implementation, there is a cost overrun in many schemes. The Central share in the total cost
 will be limited to the ceiling amount approved by the CCEA. Balance cost, if any, is to be borne by the
 respective State Government.
7.   Approved works must be completed first and where State/UTs have not been responsive enough and such works
 have been pending for more than two years because of non-action by States, a Committee of Secretaries
 consisting of Secretary Ministry of Environment & Forests, Secretary Finance, Secretary Planning Commission
 and Chief Secretary of the concerned State shall review the necessity of such schemes.
8.   National Lake Conservation Plan shall receive the same priority as the rivers.
9.   Mobilization of resources/funds will need special attention. Plan outlays would need to be enhanced substantially
 so that gap between fund requirements and outlay is bridged.
10.  Coastal towns would get special attention because it has been observed that sewage, solid waste, biomedical
 waste and the like are dumped into sea. Prioritization of coastal towns for taking up such works may be done
 from the angle of mangroves, promotion of eco-tourism, cultural and religious importance of the place and the
 like.
11.  With a view to focus on issues relating to protection and improvement and cleaning of rivers/lakes, a massive
 programme of environment education and awareness is imperative.

In recent years, there has been an increase in the number of killing of wild animals like tiger, panther, elephant, rhino, musk
 deer and other species.  Several cases of illegal export of wildlife products derived from various species have been detected
 from time to time.  This is a matter of great concern.
One of the major reasons for decline in standards of wildlife protection is the large number of vacancies at various
 level in the field formations of the Forest Department and need for greater commitment on part of the officials.  Certain
 states have made drastic cuts in the number of sanctioned posts in the Department and have also banned filling up of
 vacant posts.  Allocations to this sector have also been grossly inadequate.  There is also need for upgradation of the
 skills of the staff both in respect of prevention of wildlife crime and successful prosecution of the offenders.  An
 effective mechanism for intelligence gathering needs to be developed and steps for designating special courts for trying
 wildlife offences taken.  Further, effective infrastructure for communication, adequate mobility and sophisticated
 weapons have to be made available to the forest staff if we want  to protect and conserve our flora and fauna,
I hope after a review of the situation relating to your State, the issues mentioned above would receive your personal
 attention so that wildlife protection gets the priority it deserves.

R E P O R T
             With the setting up of Department of Biotechnology in 1986, multifarious activities for the promotion of Biotechnology and
 for creation of a strong, indigenous self-reliant base of modern biology have been carried out. The objectives of the Department
 include development of products and processes and technologies large scale application of which  would result in societal and
 economic benefits.
2.         Department of Biotechnology has sought to develop simple, easy to use, inexpensive and sensitive diagnostic kits for early
 detection of communicable and non-communicable diseases.  In the area of crop biotechnology, several Centres for Plant
 Molecular Biology (CPMBs) have been established for research in upstream areas.  In the area of horticulture and plantation crops,
 a number of Research & Development (R&D) projects have been initiated for developing complete tissue culture regeneration
 protocols for large scale multiplication of elite planting material of desired characteristics.  So far as animal biotechnology is
 concerned, major areas in which research is being pursued are – Embryo Transfer Technology (ETT), health care, diagnostics,
 nutrition, genetic resources conservation, leather biotechnology and development of       bio-products.
3.         The biotechnology programmes are being implemented through a number of autonomous and statutory institutions and
 Universities to which assistance is provided by the Department by way of grants-in-aid.  The Department is also looking after the
 work relating to the International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB).  The six autonomous institutions
 established by the department under Societies Registration Act, 1860, include:  National Institute of Immunology (NII), New Delhi;
 National Centre for Cell Science (NCCS), Pune; Centre for DNA Finger Printing and Diagnostics, Hyderabad; National Centre for
 Plant Genome Research, New Delhi; National Brain Research Centre, New Delhi.  A Public Sector undertaking namely, the Bharat
 Immunologicals and Biologicals Corporation Ltd. (BIBCOL), Bullandshahr (Uttar Pradesh) is engaged in manufacturing Oral Polio
 Vaccine (OPV) and other Immunological products under Prime Minister’s Technology Mission on Immunization, with a view to
 achieve self-sufficiency in manufacturing Oral Polio Vaccine.
4.         During the year 2001-2002, the Department has undertaken many research leads, a number of technologies were transferred
 and new initiatives taken which would yield results during the Tenth Five Year Plan (2002-07).  With the creation of the biotech
 facilities, Centres of excellence and implementation of major projects in the identified areas of national relevance, a strong base of
 biology research was established with number of expert groups in universities and national laboratories.  This would be fully
 utilized for many mission oriented and time-bound projects of crucial importance to the society and the country during the Tenth
 Plan.  The endeavour was to consolidate the research leads by initiating some mega projects in the areas of food and nutritional
 security, biofuels, stem cell research, genomic and computational biology.  In the process, establishment of biotechnology parks,
 incubators, biovillages and the programmes of societal relevance were accorded high priority. 
5.         The thrust of the Biotechnology programmes during the 9
th Plan was on basic research leading towards excellence,
 development of new products or processes, large scale demonstrations, validation and technology transfer, involvement of user
 agencies and industries, patenting and enhancing the rate of quality research publications.  Emphasis was also laid on establishing
 new Centres of excellence, facilities, programme support in priority areas, expansion of bioinformatics network and human
 resource development Centres.
6.         During the year under review, National Centre for Plant Genome Research, National Brain Research Centre and National
 Bio-Resource Development Board have been made fully operational. Major programmes on genomics which included microbial,
 structural, functional and computational genomics and DNA micro array tools to understand differential expression of genes, silk
 worm genome., sequences of chromosome 11 of rice, and sequencing of pathogens like Helicobactor pylori received a big fillip. 
 The guidelines for transgenic plants for Research and Development have been revised.  Ethical policy document on “Human
 genome, genetic research and services” has been published for use by scientists supported by the Department.  National Facility for
 Containment and Quarantine of Transgenic Planting materials, Patent Facilitating Cell, International repository authority for micro
 organisms and National facility for virus diagnosis of tissue culture raised plants have also been made operational.  Stem cell
 biology and its applications, molecular probes for oral cancer, genetic based vaccines, molecular taxonomy and Integrated Nutrient
 Management programmes have also progressed satisfactorily.  Diagnostics kits for HIV, Hepatitis-C, Dengue, Japanese
 Encephalitis, Alfafeto-protein, Hepatitis-A, reproductive hormones and banana bunchy top virus have been transferred to
 industries.  In addition, several packages for biofertilizers, plant tissue culture protocols and bioremediation technologies have also
 been given to industries for commercialization.  Recombinant candidate anthrax vaccine for use in humans is being upscaled by
 one of the industries.  DBT has supported a programme for development of low-cost nutritious food and a new mission project on
 food and nutritional security paying special attention to nutrients is under formulation.  Research projects on cancer therapy and
 diabetes are under implementation and very good progress has been achieved in the diabetes research at National Centre for Cell
 Science, Pune. 
7.         The Committee was informed that during 2002-2003, concerted efforts would be made to accomplish milestones and targets
 as enunciated in the ‘Vision Document’ which is conceptualized to attain new heights in biotechnology research, shaping
 biotechnology into a premier precision tool of the future and for creation of wealth and ensuring social justice, especially for the
 welfare of the poor. In order to integrate biotechnological research in major socio-economic sectors with a view to improve their
 productivity and efficiency and ensure environmentally sustainable development and livelihood security for the people, vigorous
 efforts would continue.  A networking approach would be followed for optimal utilization of the available infrastructure and
 generation of highly skilled human resource. 
8.         As far as the programmes/activities of the Department in North-Eastern and J&K Region are concerned, the Secretary
 informed the Committee that many programmes in the North-Eastern region in the form of R&D projects and demonstrations have

 been supported by the Department.  Recently, an Institute of Bioresource and Sustainable Development has been set up as an
 autonomous centre at Imphal, Manipur to cater to the requirements of biotechnology based development of the region.  It would
 generate the needed human resource, new technology package, and training and would take up demonstrations and technology
