9.         In J&K, two M.Sc. teaching programmes – one at University of Jammu and another at Srinagar were running well.  Some
 R&D projects in the Universities, research institutions and the medical  college  there  have been supported.  A  National Gene
 Bank  for medicinal and aromatic plants and tissue culture hardening facility has been established at Regional Research Laboratory
 (RRL), Jammu.  The tissue culture corms of saffron developed at RRL were ready for field trials.  The aim of the project was to
 provide good quality planting material.  The trials would be held in consultation with the State Department in the saffron growing
 regions of J&K.
10.        In order to create awareness abut the new technologies and activities of the Department; the Secretary informed the
 Committee that there were several mechanisms developed by the Department for transfer of technology using the services of
 NRDC and Biotech Consortium India Ltd.  Besides, there were industrial biotechnology courses running at UDCT, Bombay; IITs
 at Delhi and Kharagpur; and Anna University, Chennai to generate the needed human resource.  There are regular awareness
 programmes, workshops with the stakeholders, training programmes in tissue culture, biofertilizers etc. organized by NGOs,
 research institutions with the help of DBT.  Almost in every part of the country, Department has been organizing exhibitions where
 material in regional languages, exhibits, video films and products are displayed.  The Department is regularly bringing out bilingual
 Biotech Newsletter twice a year.  There are many other publications like Biome News, publications on Independence Day and
 Republic Day etc., which bring out from time to time, important technologies, activities and events in biotechnology.  There is a
 comprehensive website ‘www.dbtindia.org’ which gives information on various activities and programme of the Department.
11.        States of Orissa, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Karnataka have set up Biotechnology
 Boards/Department/Biotechnology Advisory Council.  Many other states were in the process of finalizing an appropriate
 institutional structure and a Biotechnology policy.  In Gujarat, a Biotechnology Advisory Council functions under the
 Chairmanship of the Chief Minister
12.        The Biotech city concept initiated at Lucknow was based on creating a networking arrangement between various research
 institutions, Govt. Departments, NGOs and industries to interact among each other and promote, support and catalyse the
 development of biotechnology.  In Lucknow, there were about 22 institutions engaged in advanced biotechnology research.  All
 these have been networked together in the concept of Biotechnology city and a website has been created at Industrial Toxicology
 Research Centre (ITRC), Lucknow which gives the total information about the expertise of these institutions.  The advantage is to
 generate inter-disciplinary, inter-institutional programmes and give a big push to the biotechnology development in the region.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
13.        The Committee was informed that the current activities of the Department namely, the human resource development,
 support for new Centres of excellence, facilities, repositories and services, basic and product oriented R&D, biotech product and
 process development, bioinformatics, international cooperation in biotechnology, biotechnology based projects for societal
 development and support to the autonomous institutions would further be consolidated and continued during the year 2002-03.
 These activities form the basis for implementation of biotechnology programmes and  development  in terms of application and
 commercialization.
14.        The total budgetary allocation (Plan & non-Plan) for the Department for the year 2002-2003 is  Rs.235.58 crores as against 
 Rs.186.34 crores in the B.E. and Rs.185.52 crores in R.E. of 2001-02.  The plan component of Rs.225 crores (for the year 2002-03)
 represents an increase of about Rs.50 crores over the B.E. & R.E. of last year. The increased amount is sought to be utilised on

16.        Asked about the income of the autonomous and public sector institutions under the control of the Department, the Secretary
 informed the Committee that autonomous institutions of the Department were mostly conducting basic research and whatever
 technologies have been transferred by them through an agreement with the industry, the revenue generated, goes back to the
 institute and part of it, as per the Government procedure, to the scientists.  The Department does not claim any share in this.  Two
 institutions namely Centre for DNA Fingerprinting & Diagnostics (CDFD), Hyderabad; and National Centre for Cell Science
 (NCCS), Pune are providing services to the scientific community for which very nominal charges are made which are ploughed
 back in the R&D efforts.  The public sector unit i.e. Bharat Immunologicals & Biologicals Corporation Ltd. (BIBCOL) is buying
 the bulk for vaccine manufacture and selling its vaccine to the M/o Health.  They are running on commercial lines and no revenue
 generated by them is given to the Department.  Last year, the profit generated out of the sale of Oral Polio Vaccine was Rs.46.60
 crore.
HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
17.        The focus of the programme has been to train a large number of highly trained scientists/students. An integrated manpower
 development programme comprising M.Sc./M.Tech./Post Doctoral course in biotechnology at various universities/ institutes of
 many states and union territories; Biotechnology national and overseas associates, short-term training courses, seminars and
 symposia, popular lectures, biology scholarships, publications and other miscellaneous programmes have been implemented.  Five
 bioscience career development awards and three women bio-scientists awards were given to eminent scientists in the year under
 review. 
18.       The Secretary informed the Committee that the method of selecting a University for starting a teaching programme in
 biotechnology was based on the scientific merit of the proposal.  A DBT-UGC joint Task Force in the DBT considers the proposals
 based on the evaluation by experts.  Generally, the DBT insists that a strong faculty and diverse expertise in biotechnology should
 be available with the University before starting a teaching programme.  The Department also provides for guest faculty from
 neighbouring institutions to enable better type of teaching programme in the absence of many well-trained faculty members.
19.       In order to encourage women scientists, DBT has instituted awards for senior and young scientists.  Besides, a special
 scheme is also under implementation for rural women through proven biotechnologies.
20.        The Committee observes that the Universities and Institutions need to play a momentous role to achieve widespread
 excellence both in terms of teaching quality and high calibre human resources. There is thus a need to strengthen existing support
 systems in the Universities and other educational institutions. Besides, DBT should also consider introducing research scholarships
 to the school leaving students in order to motivate them to join frontier areas of research in the field of biotechnology. These
 initiatives may help in accelerating the pace of biotech research for the development of a strong knowledge base and its application
 for the social welfare.
21.        The Committee is of the view that Department of Biotechnology should conduct an exercise to assess whether it would be
 in our interest  to generate a pool of critical mass of  well-trained scientific personnel for the various biotechnological research,
 training and industrial activities in the country and if so, what should be its size. To that end, if necessary, infrastructural facilities
 should be created in various scientific institutions in the country which may include germ plasm collection, animal house facilities,
 centralized facility for import and distribution of enzymes and bio-chemicals, genetic engineering units and a network of bio-
informatic systems etc.
VACCINE RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
22.        It has been stated that significant progress has been made under National Jai Vigyan Mission on developing technologies
 for vaccines for Rabies, Cholera, Malaria, Tuberculosis, Japanese Encephalitis and HIV infections.  A formulation consisting of
 Deoxyribo Nucleic Acid (DNA) and small amount of protein from the tissue cultured grown Rabies virus has completed trials in
 dogs and cattle’s. It is being upscaled and is likely to be made available soon in the market to control rabies in dogs.  The HIV
 DNA candidate vaccine has completed its immunogenicity in small laboratory animals and is currently under going
 immunogenicity and preclinical toxicology in non-human primates.  The tissue cultured Japanese Encephalitis candidate vaccine
 elicited about 70% protection in animals following intracereberal challenge.  The technology is ready to replace the existing
 Japanese Encephalitis Vaccine.  Five DNA candidate vaccines as alternative to BCG to control tuberculosis have completed their
 immunogenicity investigations. A Laboratory Scale GMP (Good Manufacturing Practice) facility for the production of recombinant
 proteins to be used as malaria vaccine candidate is also functional.
23.        The Committee was informed that three diagnostics for HIV/AIDS have been developed, validated and found to have very
 high degree of sensitivity and specificity.  Two of the diagnostic test systems namely, the Western Immunoblot Assay and Naked
 Eye Visible Agglutination Assay (NEVA) have been transferred to industries.  The industries have refined, upscaled and launched
 these in the market after obtaining appropriate approval from the Drugs Controller General of India.  The western immunoblot
 assay confirms the HIV infections while NEVA utilizing recombinant chemeric reagents yields results with 1-2 minutes.  Both of
 these test systems have sensitivity of 99.8% with the specificity of 99.6%.  Another diagnostic test, peptide ELISA system for
 diagnosis of HIV, has been validated and was transferred to one of the Indian industries, namely M/s Ace Diagnostics, Delhi. 
 Before  the industry  could launch the product in the market, the company was wound up. The Department is again negotiating with
 other industries for taking up the technology.
24.        The contraceptive vaccine to control fertility in females, namely, the B hCG completed its phase-II clinical trials.  The
 analysis of the idea suggested that some more basic studies are required for enhanced and sustainable immune responses in
 vaccines.  A new formulation that provides relatively better-enhanced and sustainable immune response has been evaluated in
 animals.  It needs to be further validated in non-human primates and if found effective, the formulation will undergo clinical trials. 
 The oFSH candidate vaccine as a male anti fertility candidate vaccine underwent phase-I clinical trials.  The data of the trials
 indicated changes in the hormonal parameters in individuals that received vaccine.  The work on Riboflavin Carrier Protein (RCP)

hhhh
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/99th.htm[29-08-2018 16:20:38]
 is continuing and now the recombinant sub units of the same were being evaluated.  The experimental studies suggested RCP has
 efficacy as anti fertility candidate both for males & females.  More studies in assessing the efficacy of the recombinant subunit in
 primates have been planned.
25.        The DBT was involved with the development of vaccines and diagnostics.  A technique for development of ‘Artether’ from
 artimisia (medicinal plant) has been standardized at Central Institute of Medicinal & Aromatic Plants(CIMAP), Lucknow.  Efforts
 were on to transfer the technology to an industry. AIDS diagnostic kits – a peptide based ELISA was also developed and
 transferred to M/s Ace Diagnostics which has since been closed down.  Negotiations with other industries have been conducted to
 transfer this technology.  However, a western blot and NEVA – a quick test has already been given to the industry and were now
 available in the market.
26.       The Committee commends the efforts being made by the Department in vaccine research and development.  The Committee
 is of the view that much needs to be done to contain major infectious diseases like tuberculosis, malaria, Japanese encephalitis, as
 well as, non-communicable diseases like hormonal disorders.  The Committee notes with satisfaction that the diagnostic kits would
 be made available in the market this year. Besides, vaccine for rabies, cholera, HIV, TB, malaria and Japanese encephalitis should
 be ready in the next couple of years.  The Committee hopes that the vaccines/medicines would be priced reasonably so that they are
 within the reach of larger sections of the society.
AUTONOMOUS INSTITTIONS
27.        The Department has under its control five autonomous institutions namely National Institute of Immunology, New Delhi;
 National Centre for Cell Science, Pune;  Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics, Hyderabad; National Centre for Plant
 Genome Research and National Brain Research Centre in New Delhi.  These institutions are involved in pursuing basic and applied
 research leading to generation of new knowledge, products, patents and publication of papers with high impact factor.  An Institute
 of Bio-resources and Sustainable Development (IBSD) has been established last year at Imphal, Manipur in order to develop and
 utilize the rich bio-resources of North East India, using tools of Biotechnology.
National Institute Of Immunology
28.        The National Institute of Immunology (NII) is working at furthering knowledge of the molecular mechanisms of interaction
 between the biological systems and their environment while searching for new intervention modalities to combat mortality and
 morbidity. The range of areas being explored at NII focus around the cellular cross-talks, parasitic targets and the precise
 modulation of bodily defense mechanisms, which have,  over the years, coalesced into four major themes; immunity and infection,
 gene regulation, molecular design and reproduction & development..
29.        While the Institute continues to work on four major themes as mentioned above. Japanese Encephalitis Virus (JEV)
 envelope protein together with the pre-membrane protein, delivered to mice by intramuscular injection or using a gene gun have
 shown good immunological responses. The studies using ribozyme approach have provided important clues on the course of HIV-
1, HIV-2 and Simian Immuno Deficiency Virus (SIV) infection  and  disease  pattern.  As part of the studies on molecular
 modelling of peptides and protein-ligand complexes a quick screening tool to identify potential MHC (an antibody) binding
 sequences and simple approach to predict peptide conformations in the MHC groove with a reasonable accuracy have been
 established. Three technological leads were granted international patents and three other Indian patents.
30.        The Committee was informed that enhanced budgetary allocation in this year was made to initiate the work of Incubator
 laboratory facility in the second campus of the National Institute of Immunology to help the biotechnology industry and upgrade
 animal facility and set up election/scanning microscopic facility.  In addition, specific cutting edge research programmes relating to
 identification of novel tissue specific gene by exploiting the genomic revolution would be undertaken in order to address
 fundamental biological issues.
31.        The Committee has also been informed that the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare has been apprised about the potential
 and utility of the Mw anti leprosy vaccine for inclusion in the National Leprosy Control Programme.  However, about 2.7 lakh
 doses have been supplied free of cost to various hospitals and leprosy homes.  LAPROVAC has been given to various stockists in
 Maharashtra, Gujarat, Bihar, Orissa, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Chandigarh.
Centre for DNA Fingerprinting & Diagnostics
32.        The Centre for DNA Fingerprinting & Diagnostics (CDFD) continues to provide services for DNA fingerprinting,
 diagnostics, bio-informatics and automated genome analysis and concentrated research & development in the area of genetics,
 molecular & cellular biology, molecular pathogenesis and bio-informatics. During the year 2001-02, the Centre has received a total
 of 201 cases for DNA fingerprinting examination. Of these, 85 cases were for establishment of paternity, 75 for identification of
 individuals, 33 involving rape, 2 for determining biological relationships, 5 for wildlife identification and one for plant
 identification. In order to provide services for diagnosis, the Centre has received a total of 1820 referral cases against 490 last year
 which represent a jump of over 370%. The Centre has screened 4180 newborn children under “New Born Screening Programme”
 for common inborn errors of metabolism.
33.        As revealed in the Background Note submitted by the Department during the examination of Demands for Grants (2002-
03), an agreement has been signed between CDFD and the Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) for developing niche software in
 Bioinformatics, train a select group of TCS employees and conduct long-term R&D. Besides, the Centre has identified several
 DNA polymorphisms in Helicobacter pylori that distinguish strains from Asia and Europe. The genotypic signatures for all the
 pathogenic strains have been generated using universal Amplified Fragment Length Polymorphism (AFLP) approach of Keygene
 and Applied Biosystems. Using “Automated Genome Analysis Facility”, the Centre has carried out large scale genome sequencing
 of human DNA samples for retinoblastoma gene (rb1) mutations and CYP1B1 gene mutations associated with glaucoma. Basmati
 specific markers which discriminate pure lines from the evolved Basmati and non- Basmati rice varieties have also been identified.
34.        In reply to the question about the decline in the allocation for the Centre for the year 2002-03, the Committee was informed
 that as per the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) provision, the CDFD would require an amount of Rs.9.90 crores during the

 to the department.  The Department is in the process of revising earlier EFC provisions and would seek additional funds during

35.        The Committee undertook a visit to CDFD on 27th December, 2001 in order to study the functioning and programmes of
 the Centre. The Committee was informed about the work being done by the Centre for DNA fingerprinting, disease diagnosis and
 other services. The new born screening program whereby every child born in the Government hospitals in the city of Hyderabad for
 metabolic errors, was applauded by Committee whereby techniques of modern biology were being applied for betterment of human
 kind. The Committee was also apprised about the research work being carried out leading to several new findings, particularly the
 development of new Hybrid varieties of silk work with improved commercial traits, identification of the gene for childhood
 blindness, molecular typing of the tuberculosis bacterium and the one that causes gastric cancer and gastric ulcer, regulation of
 genes in both bacteria and viruses and the development of clinical-informatics databases. 
36.       The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Centre for DNA Fingerprinting & Diagnostics (CDFD) has emerged as a
 Centre of Excellence.The Centre has been delivering a range of services relating to modern biology even though it is operating
 from a rentedbuilding. The Committee, therefore, is of the view that maximum support should be provided to the Centre so as to
 reinforce the unique synthesis of services and research being carried out by CDFD. The Centre should be encouraged to have its
 own building.  To that end the Department should help it with adequate funds so that its planned projects on Genome analysis, Bio-
terrorism & Bioinformatics do not suffer.
National Brain Research Centre
37.            National Brain Research Centre (NBRC), Gurgoan is undertaking multidisciplinary research on neurosciences to
 understand brain function encompassing relating genes to cognition, from molecules to mind. NBRC has worked towards achieving
 these objectives through the state-of-art facilities. Efforts are on to support and network the existing groups in the country and
 provide comprehensive training and teaching in neuroscience.
38.        The Committee was informed that the research on several parameters of neurosciences namely, dynamic control of saccade
 target selection; Mitochondrial dysfunction and protein thiol homeostasis in neurodegenerative diseases; Psychoactive drug
 metabolism by brain cytochromes P-450 and mechanisms of neuronal stem cell differentiation have been initiated at the NBRC,
 Gurgoan. Two Indo-US Workshops were held to promote research collaboration through the MoU signed between National
 Institute of Mental Health, USA and NBRC, India.
39.       The Committee feels the need for coordination between the research activities undertaken at National Brain Research Centre
 (NBRC), Gurgoan and for their knowledge/application etc. to the neurologists so that they can optimally apply the same while
 treating brain related cases. To that end, workshops must also be conducted at regular intervals in order to apprise Medical colleges
 and concerned departments in neurology about the research findings with a view to improve patient care. 
 BIOTECHNOLOGY PATENT FACILITATING CELL
40.        The Biotechnology Patent Facilitating Cell (BPFC) is working towards the creation of awareness and understanding relating
 to patents among scientists by arranging workshops, seminars, conferences, providing patenting facilities to biotechnologists in the
 country for filing Indian and international patents on a continuous basis and make important issues known to policy makers, bio-
scientists, biotech industry, etc. The patent cell has streamlined the process of patent facilitation and has created patent search
 capabilities within the Department for conducting preliminary patent search for rigorous assessment of the inventions received at
 the Department for patenting.
41.        The Committee was informed that during 2001-02, 13 new patent applications have been received and six applications have
 been filed through Patent Co-operation Treaty (PCT). One Indian and one US patent have been granted. A total of 99 patents have
 been filed by the Department so far.
42.       The Committee recommends the Department to refurbish the system for protecting intellectual property rights in the
 booming biotechnology sector. In order to achieve its set targets, the Department should take initiatives to frame appropriate
 strategies and policies to maximize the benefits and minimize the disadvantages from the post General Agreement on Trade &
 Tariffs-Intellectual Property Rights (GATT-IPR) regime. The Department should also launch a major well-directed plan, with
 significant investment, for harnessing biotech tools for generation of products, processes and technologies.
43.       The Committee is also of the view that the complete procedure for filing applications for patents and patents etc.
 already granted should be available on the web-site, if not already available, to help the prospective applicants.
BIO-INFORMATICS
44.        The plan scheme of bio-informatics envisages to provide a National Bio-informatics Network in the country designed to
 bridge the gaps in Biotechnology information and to establish links among scientists in Biotechnology.  The network aims to
 provide a single reference to various information resources of importance to biotechnology and modern biology including data
 banks of genetic importance published literature, patents and other information of scientific and commercial value.  It also aims to
 provide necessary infrastructural support for modern research in biology involving computationally intensive analysis.  The
 network consists of 11 Distributed Information Centers (DICs) and 45 sub-DICs computational facilities at the national level.  It
 has also established linkages with international institutions like International Centre for Co-operation in Bio-informatics (ICCB), a
 UNESCO based funded bio-informatics programme and is also linked with EMB net, as well as international legume-data base and
 information services (ILDIS).  Educational and training activities in bio-informatics will also form part of the scheme.  National Jai
 Vigyan Mission on Mirror Sites for Genomic Research to establish four major databases at Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore;
 University of Pune; Jawaharlal Nehru University and Institute of Microbial Technology, Chandigarh have progressed well.  New
 projects for establishing Centres of excellence in bio-informatics will be taken up.

45.       The Committee was informed that the on-going Bioinformatics network has 57 Bioinformatics centres spread across the
 country at various research institutions/universities.  Each centre of the network has built up Bioinformatics resources in their
 specialized areas in the form of databases,  software packages for  application to Biotechnology  and  Molecular Biology. 
These are shared over the network by the researchers in the country.  Towards the development of molecular modelling and
 simulation studies in biotechnology, six interactive graphic facilities have been established and they act as a National facility for
 the benefit of researchers in the country.  Four one-year Post-graduate Diploma courses on Bioinformatics are being offered by
 major universities with a view to enhance human resource in the field.  Every year more than 50 short-term training programmes
 are being conducted to provide awareness towards the utilization of Bioinformatics resources.  Under the National Jai Vigyan
 Science & Technology Mission, mirror sites of internationally recognized databases have been established for unhindered access to
 large amount information resources for the acceleration of R&D activities in genomics and proteomics.
46.            Besides, continuation of the ongoing activities during 2002-03, the emphasis will be on augmenting the Centres and
 development of new tools.  Five more Bioinformatics Centres are proposed to be set up as part of the network.  Mirroring of some
 important databases like celera genomics is also proposed to be undertaken.  Preparatory work has already been completed for the
 establishment of a high speed Virtual Private Network (VPN).  It is also proposed to support the M.Tech programme in
 Bioinformtics and other manpower development activities.  Important research leads are expected to arise through the use of
 Bioinformatics resources.  The network will act as knowledge pathway for the discoveries in Biotechnology and Molecular
 Biology.  The proposed new initiatives are designed to add value to the existing network and available resources will be utilized for
 the same through prioritization.  
47.       The Committee observes that it is necessary to augment the Biotech network with a view to exploit the germplasm
 base and vast pool of talented bioinformatics scientists and low cost software skills.  Department of Biotechnology should
 undertake an exercise to ascertain how far the exploitation is desirable & feasible.  Thereafter, if necessary, the Department
 should establish more Centres for high areas of research and development, functional genomics microarray and structural
 genomics and for creating infrastructure. The Government support should be kept at minimal and more and more
 industrial interface should be supported/enhanced. The Department should also bolster the bioinformatics education
 through publication of bioinformatics textbooks and monographs by reputed scientists in the field.
48.       The Committee is of the view that in order to fulfil the growing need for latest information, Biotechnology Information
 Network should also be established to work as a distributed database and network organisation in order to provide an integrated
 information resource on all aspects of biotechnology, that will provide bio-informatics and bio-computing services to
 researchers and manufacturing activities.
MEDICAL BIOTECHNOLOGY
49.        Medical Biotechnology has come to a centre stage with spectacular advances in biology. This is due to a number of
 emerging and re-emerging infections requiring immediate attention for development of suitable diagnostics and therapeutics.
 Several events at the international biotech scene such as the rise of genomics era, stem cell research and bioinformatics have
 percolated down to the national biotechnology scene with a large number of scientists galvanized to reap the benefits. The
 Department of Biotechnology has continued its efforts for the development of suitable diagnostics, vaccines, therapeutic and better
 drug delivery systems. 
50.        The Committee was informed that three Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) based diagnostics for tuberculosis have been
 validated and are ready for commercialistion. A new probe indicating multi drug resistance for Mycobacterium tuberculosis
 infection is undergoing evaluation. Moreover a unique mechanism of transport of anti malaria drug has led to identification of 65
 KDA molecules as a possible new drug target. Major programmes on stem cell biology and applications have been implemented at
 LV Prasad Eye Institute at Hyderabad, National Brain Research Centre, Gurgoan and Christian Medical College, Vellore. A multi
 centric programme on oral cancer to identify molecular probes for early detection and possible markers for progression and
 prognosis of the oral cancer has also been implemented.  Twenty-one diagnostics technologies have been developed and twelve
 have been transferred to industries for upscaling and commercialization. Two HIV diagnostics test systems and one Hepatitis-C
 diagnostics test system has been launched in the market. As a collaborative effort, the scientists at Deccan College of Medical
 College of Medical Sciences, Hyderabad along with industries have been able to sequence the whole genome of one of the Indian
 isolate of Hepatitis C. This is the first effort made by Indian scientists to sequence a microbe relevant to the country.
51.        The Background Note on Demands for Grants (2002-03) for the Department contains the information that seventeen
 prototype diagnostic test systems and other bio-medical technologies relating to vaccines have been transferred to industries. Of
 these, five namely: Leprosy Immunomodulator; Leshmanisis detection Kit; Western Blot for HIV-I & II; Naked eye agglutination
 system for HIV I & II; and ELISA based Hepatitis-C diagnostics have been launched by the industries.
52.        Twelve technologies transferred to the industries are in the process of upscaling and refinement for commercial use.  These
 are : The lgM Mac ELISA for the detection for Dengue, Japanese Encephalitis,  West Nile, ELISA system to measure alpha-feto
 protein levels in pregnant women, An lgM based system for the detection of Hepatitis.  A virus using monoclonal/polyclonal
 antibodies, Urine based system (ELISA) for the detection of four reproductive hormones, a technology utilizing Yerrowia lipolytica
 expressing Hepatitis B surface and pre S genes, a technology for expressing  hCG using Pichia pastoris and Recombinant
 candidate Anthrax vaccine. In addition, eleven other technologies have been developed and some have already undergone
 validations.  The Department is in the process of transferring these to industry.

 BIOTECHNOLOGY FOR SOCIETAL DEVELOPMENT
55.        The objective of the programme is to provide biotechnology tools/products to benefit SC/ST population and empowerment
 of women for their economic development. The programmes on rural areas are stated to have benefited around 10,000 rural
 people.  More than 2,000 rural people have been trained to cultivate medicinal plants.  Many more people have also been trained in
 preparation of products like Jams, Jelly, squash, pickle and these products are being sold in local market.  24 projects on
 biotechnology involving women were supported in 11 States and Union Territories. These projects have resulted in training of
 women for entrepreneurship development in various areas such as food processing, sericulture, mushroom cultivation, micro
 propagation or orchids and other ornamental plants, biofertilizer production, goat and poultry rearing, fish farming, rabbit rearing
 for quality wool production and establishment of nurseries of medicinal and aromatic plants as well as formulation of certain herbal
 products. So far, around 8000 women are stated to have benefited from the programme.  A total of 102 projects have been
 supported in 20 States and Union Territories benefiting about 15,000 families under the programme for SC/ST.  The programmes
 were started with the objective of creating awareness on biotechnology packages for income generation and better healthcare, using
 biotechnological processes and tools for creating new avenues of employment and promoting bio-village concept for socio-
economic upliftment of target population in rural area and women and SC/ST.     
56.        The Committee commends the efforts made by the Department for upliftment of SC/ST population and women. The
 Committee feels that Department should publicise their entrepreneurship programmes so that concerned companies could come
 forward for marketing their products through these communities. The Department   may also consider taking initiatives to motivate
 the Khadi & Village Industries Commission (KVIC) or similar bodies to provide their products and market them through their
 stores.
BIOLOGICAL CONTROL OF PLANT PESTS, DISEASES AND WEEDS
57.        The Committee was informed that effective modules/packages that are cost effective, sustainable and eco-friendly have
 been developed by the Department through a network programme on Integrated Pest Management and Integrated Nutrient
 Management for increasing agriculture productivity in existing cropping systems of various agro-climatic zones. About 50,000
 have farmers have benefited through training programmes and extension activities and around 1600 handouts in regional languages
 were released.  Several biopesticide technologies have also been developed based on the large-scale field efficacy. Patents have
 also been filed for the mass production technologies of biocontrol agents and their product formulations.
58.       The Committee notes with satisfaction the achievements made by the Department in the field of biological control of plant
 pests, diseases and weeds. However, it would like to add a note of caution that before undertaking large scale production, proper
 field tests must be conducted to pre-empt any controversy.
INTERNATIONAL COLLABORATIONS
59.            International Collaboration in Biotechnology received major thrust in advanced areas of research in medical, agricultural
 and environmental fields aimed at updating and advancing the state-of-the-art research facilities in the country through promotion
 of bilateral as well as multilateral collaborations. The collaborations included adaptation of latest technologies complementary to
 the  research and  development work  with the most advanced  countries to the mutual benefit. The important ones include: Indo-
US collaboration research; collaboration with Switzerland, Sweden and Germany and with Russia where the collaboration has led to
 establishment of a research Centre at Allahabad. The Department has been working in specific areas with Tunisia, Israel, Belarus
 and Sri Lanka.  Progamme with China and Poland are also under progress.  As a result, there is much greater exchange of scientists
 thus providing opportunities to young scientists from India to work in some of the best laboratories abroad. 
60.        The autonomous institutions of the Department have also been an integral part in the international collaboration.  The
 National Brain Research Centre had the first scientific event under the Indo-US forum where an Indo-US workshop in brain
 research in the country was organised.  The Department has specially provided help to Myanmar and Syria for development of
 biotechnology initiatives, institutions and research programmes.
61.        A network project on development of pro-vitamin-A rich rice under Indo-Swiss collaboration in biotechnology has also
 been approved.  Future collaborations are being identified with European Union and Scandinavian and Latin American countries,
 Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore including strengthening SAARC cooperation.
62.            International cooperation is pursued for adaptation of latest technology complimentary to the R&D work with the most
 advanced countries for mutual benefit.  It helps in implementation of national R&D programmes and to open up avenues for
 collaborative interaction in advanced areas leading to transfer of technologies/knowledge into the country.  This has already
 provided training to a large number of young scientists and helped in the development of products and processes, for example
 development of a new process for lactic acid production, biosensors, tissue culture protocols, cryo preservation to teak, and
 development of vaccine for rota viral diarrhea.  Under material transfer agreements in different joint projects, gene constructs,
 reagents, protocols, sophisticated equipment, tools and techniques have also been made available to Indian laboratories.  Several
 interactive workshops and seminars have added value to the knowledge base.  Financial support from some of these collaborations
 to the Indian laboratories is to the tune of about Rs.20 crores.
63.       The Committee feels that all efforts for bilateral cooperation must aim at developing better research facilities in India. It
 should be the continuous endeavour of the Department to provide world-class research conditions so as to stop brain drain and

STEM CELLS
64.        Stem Cell has been identified as a potential area of research. The development of stem cell lines that may produce many
 human tissues would revolutionalise the practice of medicine and improve the quality and longevity of life. According to News
 Reports researchers at John Hunters Hospital in New South Wales were said to be using adult stem cells to repair  a man’s
 damaged  heart tissue.  They took stem cells from bone  marrow in the man’s hip and injected them into his heart.  In what is
 described as a world’s first, they hope, they would grow into new blood vessels.  It would take about a year to see if the trial is
 successful.  Potentially it could be used to treat almost a third of patients with     end-stage coronary artery disease.
65.        In 2000, the Department had organized a Brain Storming Session on “Stem Cell Biology and its Applications” to develop
 programmes on biology and clinical use of stem cells and related ethical issues. Basic areas identified in session are understanding
 the basic biology of stem cells, banking and characterization of stem cells, utility of stem cells for organogenesis & gene therapy.
 66.        In response to a question about the Department’s awareness of the reservations expressed by  countries notably Germany
 on red gene technology which deals with stem cells and as a result thereof  moratorium in the European Union and  ban imposed by
 the Germany on stem cell research, the Committee was informed that  Stem cells especially embryonic stem cells have great
 potential in generating tissues for cell therapies for disorders like Parkinson’s Aizheimer, Diabetes, Cardiac muscles, Cardio-
vascular disorders, bones & cartages and haemoglobinopathies. While India has permitted the use of both adult & embryonic stem
 cells for therapeutic purposes only, Germany initially permitted the research on imported embryonic stem cells.  But it has now
 banned this.  The Department was aware of the concerns of Germany and other European countries.  These countries fear that such
 programmes represent the first step towards embarking on reproduction cloning and germline interventions.  However, as per the
 ethical document entitled “Ethical Policies on Human Genome, Genetic Research and Services” prepared by the “National
 Bioethics Committee” of the Department of Biotechnology any research on human cloning and germline interventions by Indian
 investigators, was banned.

 important programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Budgetary allocation of Rs.
 235.58 crores, as sought by the Department of Biotechnology for the year 2002-2003, under Demand No. 72, may be
 approved.

R E P O R T 
 
CHAPTER I 
REIVIEW OF STATUS OF IMPLEMENTATION OF RECOMMENDATIONS  
CONTAINED IN THE THIRTY-THIRD REPORT OF THE STANDING COMMITTEE ON 
SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT ON DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2008 -2009) 
OF THE MINISTRY OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT 
 
 
1.1 The Thirty -third Report of the Standing Committee on Social Justice and 
Empowerment on Demands for Grants (2008 -2009) pertaining to the Ministry of Social 
Justice and Empowerment was presented to Lok Sabha and laid in Rajya Sabha on 
21.04.2008.  The Action Taken Report (Forty -first Report, Fourteenth Lok Sabha), on 
the recommendations contained in the Thirty -third Report was presented to Parliament 
on 19.12.2008. 
 
1.2 The Thirty -third Report contained 13 recommendations, out of which the 
Government accepted 7 recommendations.  In view of the replies of the Government 
the Committee did not desire to pursue 1 recommendation, 2 recommendations were 
commented upon by the Committee and 3 replies of the Government with respect to the 
recommendations of the Committee were interim in nature. 
 
1.3 The Minister of Social Justice and E mpowerment laid a statement in Parliament 
under Direction 73A on 18.12.2008 on the status of implementation of the 
recommendations contained in the Thirty-third Report of the Committee on Demands for 
Grants (2008 -09). Out of the 13 recommendations, 4 recommendations (Sl. Nos. 
6,9,11&13)  have been implemented by the Government, 8 recommendations (Sl. Nos. 
1,2,3,5,7,8,10&12) are under the process of implementation and 1 recommendation (Sl. 
No. 4) has not been implemented by the Government.  

8 
 
1.4 The Committee  are not satisfied with the implementation aspect of the 
Recommendations contained in their Thirty -third Report on Demands for Grants, 
2008-09 of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment as only 4 out of 13 
recommendations have been implemented.  The  Committee desire expeditious 
implementation of the remaining  recommendations already accepted by the 
Government.  

9 
 
CHAPTER – II 
INTRODUCTORY 
 
2.1 The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment have informed the Committee 
that this Ministry is responsible for looking after the welfare of the disadvantaged and 
marginalized sections of society such as Scheduled Castes, Other Backward Classes, 
Senior Citizens, Persons with Disability and Victims of Substance Abuse .  The basic 
objective of policies, programmes,  laws and institutions of the Indian Welfare System is 
to bring the target -groups into the mainstream of development by making them self -
reliant.  In achieving this objective, the Ministry performs the task of implementation in 
accordance with the provisio ns under Chapter III and Chapter IV of the Constitution, 
which deal with the development and welfare of the disadvantaged and marginalized 
groups mentioned above and also give a concept of justice to include social and 
distributive aspects. 
 Target Groups: Persons belonging to:- 
a. Scheduled Castes 
b. Other Backward Classes 
c. Persons with Disabilities  
d. Senior Citizens and 
e. Victims of Substance Abuse 
 Goals 
a Educational Development 
b. Economic Development 
c. Social Empowerment 

10 
 
d. Rehabilitation 
e.  Manpower Development 
Policy Framework 
2.2 As per the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, its Policy framework is 
welfare schemes for development of persons belonging to socially disadvantaged 
groups such as Scheduled Castes, Other Backward Classes,  Persons with Disabilities, 
Senior Citizens and Victims of Substance Abuse  and the same is implemented through 
State Governments/UT Administrations, and voluntary organizations.  Public -Private 
partnership is encouraged in the process.  Education being a S tate subject, State 
Governments/UT Administrations are involved in meeting educational needs of these 
groups.  This is achieved by way of providing scholarships, hostels, coaching, fellowship 
and assistance to children belonging to the target groups beginn ing from Class I 
onwards.  The ultimate objective is to increase the literacy rate among them and also 
girl students so as to bring them at par with general population.  Similarly, Finance and 
Development Corporations provide credit facilities for various income-generating 
activities towards economic self -reliance.  Mahila Samridhi Yojana is also implemented 
by these Corporations. National Institutes dealing with Disabilities and Social Defence 
conduct short -term & long -term programmes for various levels of  personnel.  These 
Institutes also do research in their areas and provide services such as education and 
vocational training . Voluntary organizations are also given grants for implementing 
programmes in the distant areas. 
2.3 According to the Government of  India Allocation of Business Rules 1961 the 
mandate of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is as follows : 
 Development of Scheduled Castes and Other Backward Classes; 

11 
 
 Scheduled Castes and Other Backward Classes including Scholarships to 
students belonging to such castes and classes; 
 Reports of the Commission to investigate into conditions of Backwards;  
 Education, training, rehabilitation and welfare of the physically and 
mentally handicapped; 
 Convention with other countries in matters relating to social defence and 
references from United Nations Organization relating to prevention of 
crime and treatment of offenders; 
 Social and Moral Hygiene Programme; 
 Beggary; 
 All ma tters relating to alcoholism and substance (drug) abuse and 
rehabilitation of addicts/families; 
 Promotion of efforts including voluntary efforts to ensure the well being of 
the older persons; 
 All matters relating to prohibition;  
 Educational and social welfare aspects of drug addiction; 
 Charitable and religious endowments pertaining to subjects allocated to 
this Ministry; 
 Social Welfare, Social Welfare Planning, Project formulation, research 
evaluation, statistics and training; 
 Research, evaluation, training, exchange of information and technical 
guidance on all social defence matters; 
 
2.4 The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is divided into the following 
Divisions. 
 Scheduled Castes Development 
 Backward Classes Development 
 Disability  
 Social Defence 
 
2.5 Implementation of the following Acts is the responsibility of the Ministry:-  

12 
 
  
 Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the Scheduled Castes and the 
Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 
 The Rehabilitation Council of India Act, 1992 (34 of 1992) 
 National Commission for Backward Classes Act, 1993 
 The Pe rsons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights 
and Full Participation) Act, 1995 (01 of 1996) 
 The National Trust for Welfare of Persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, 
Mental Retardation and Multiple Disabilities Act, 1999 (44 of 1999). 
 The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007. 
 
2.6 The Ministry gets specialized and technical inputs from 8 National Institutes and 
apex level organizations, namely; 
 National Institute of Social Defence, New Delhi 
 National Institute for Visually Handicapped, Dehradun 
 National Institute for Mentally Handicapped, Secunderabad 
 National Institute for Hearing Handicapped, Mumbai 
 National Institute for Orthopaedically Handicapped, Kolkata 
 National Institute for Rehabilitation, Training & Research, Cuttack 
 Deen Dayal Institute for Physically Handicapped, New Delhi 
 National Institute for Multiple  Handicapped, Chennai 
2.7 The activities of the following National Commissions come under the purview of 
the Ministry: 
 National Commission for Scheduled Castes 
 National Commission for Safai Karamcharis 
 National Commission for Backward Classes 
 National Commission for Denotified, Nomadic and Semi-nomadic Tribes  
 Commission for Economically Backward Classes  
 National Commission for Sub-categorization of Scheduled  Castes in 
Andhra Pradesh  

13 
 
2.8 In order to provide for necessary statutory coverage to persons with disabilities, 
the Ministry has set up three statutory bodies: 
 
 Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities 
 National Trust for the Welfare of Persons with Autism, Cerebral Palsy, 
Mental Retardation and Multiple Disabilities; and 
 Rehabilitation Council of India 
 
2.9 With a view to give an impetus to the special needs of the weaker and vulnerable 
sections of society, the following five Finance & Development Corporations have been 
set up by the Ministry under Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956 : 
 National Scheduled Castes Finance & Development Corporation. 
 National Safai Karamcharis Finance & Development Corporation. 
 National Backward Classes Finance and Development Corporation. 
 National Handicapped Finance & Development Corporation.

3.21 The Committee observe that the Ministry of Social Justice and 
Empowerment has not received adequate attention of the Planning Commission 
as far as the budgetary allocation is concerne d. A quick glance at the  combined 
figures both Plan and Non -Plan reveals that while annual budgetary allocation to 
the Ministry was Rs. 2200 crore in  the year 2007 -08, it has increased only 
marginally to Rs. 2400 crore in 2008-09 and then to Rs. 2500 crore during 2009-10. 
The Committee feel  that this token increase in the allocation to the Ministry over 
the past three years does not correspond with the  budgetary/resource 
requirement under various schemes being implemented by the Ministry.  The 
Committee are given to understand that as against an amount of Rs. 5000 crore 
asked for by the Ministry in its annual plan proposals, the Planning Commission 
have sanctioned only half of the amount.  The Ministry have learnt that the 
Planning Commission did not consider the budgetary allocation of this Ministry 
to the extent asked for as the requirements of flagship schemes such as Sarva 
Shiksha Abiyan, ICDS , NREGP etc. under other Ministries were so huge that it 
was not possible  to accommodate the request of Ministry of Social Justice and 

25 
 
Empowerment for higher allocation  during 2009 -10.  Though the Ministry have 
maintained that they have made strenuous efforts in persuading the Planning 
Commission for increased budgetary allocation, the Committee feel that the 
Ministry have failed to convince the Planning Commission for increased 
allocation.  This is more so because if the requirement of other poverty alleviation 
schemes is huge as per Planning Commission’s reasoning, it is with the same 
logic that the budgetary allocation of this Ministry should be stepped up as the 
target group of this Ministry is more than 60% of the country’s population 
covering various disadvan taged sections of the society. Being a large Ministry 
with vast jurisdiction of work , it  has to cater to the multifaceted developmental 
needs of large sections of the society such as SCs, OBCs, People with 
Disabilities, Senior Citizens and victims of drug abuse.  The financial allocation 
under both plan and non -plan heads is not commensurate with the mandate of 
the Ministry. Therefore, the Committee recommend that the Ministry should gear 
up its machinery and approach the Planning Commission in a more  convincing 
and forceful manner for an enhanced allocation urgently so as to enable them to 
fulfill their mandate resourcefully and more effectively.   The Committee desire 
that in case the Planning Commission remains unconvinced, the detailed 
response of the Commission may be sent to the Committee for examination.  
  
3.22 The Committee are distressed to note that some of the very important and 
core schemes of the Ministry such as Special Central Assistance to Scheduled 
Castes Sub -Plan, Deen Dayal Disabled Rehabilitation Scheme, the Scheme of 
Assistance to Disabled for Purchase/Fitting of Aids and Appliances , Post-Matric

affected due to non-increase in the budgetary allocation of th e Ministry as well as

Scholarship for all Scheduled Caste students for which the Planning Commission 
has already given in principle approval could not take off till now because of

of schemes are high and resources required to meet the need under various 
schemes are huge whereas the actual amount sanctioned to the Ministry by the 
Government of India is grossly inadequate.  The Ministry are also not taking the 
schemes seriously and  not paying the requisite attention to its schemes on the

critical input for social justice and empowerment, especially  in a context where

CHAPTER IV 
DEVELOPMENT OF SCHEDULED CASTES 
A. SPECIAL CENTRAL ASSISTANCE (SCA) TO SCHEDULED CASTES SUB -
PLAN (SCSP) 
I  Scheduled Castes Sub-Plan (SCSP) 
 
 
4.1 The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is the nodal Ministry to oversee 
the interests of the Scheduled Castes.  Though the primary responsibility for promotion 
of interest of Scheduled Castes rests with all the Central Ministries in the areas of th eir 
operations and the State Governments, the Ministry of Social Justice and 
Empowerment complements their efforts by way of interventions in critical sectors 
through specifically tailored schemes.  The Ministry also monitors the efforts taken by 
State Governments and Central Ministries for protecting and promoting the interests of 
Scheduled Castes.   
4.2 The special Component Plan for Scheduled Castes evolved in 1979 has been 
renamed as Scheduled Castes Sub -Plan (SCSP).  The strategy of Scheduled Castes 
Sub-Plan is one of the most important interventions through the planning process for 
social, economic and educational development of Scheduled Castes and also for 
improvement in their working and living conditions.  Scheduled Castes Sub-Plan is not a 
scheme by itself.  It is an umbrella strategy to ensure flow of targeted financial and 
physical benefits from all the general sectors of development for the benefit of 
Scheduled Castes.  Under this strategy, States/UTs and Central Ministries are required 
to formulate and implement Scheduled Castes Sub -Plan as part of their Annual Plans 
by earmarking resources in proportion to their share in total population.

C. BABU JAGJIVAN RAM CHHATRAWAS YOJNA 
 
4.28 The centrally sponsored scheme of hostels for SC boys and girls has been revised 
and reanmed as “Babu Jagjivan Ram Chhatrawas Yojana” w.e.f. 01.01.2008.  There are 
two components under the scheme – Boys Hostel and Girls Hostels.  The objective of the 
Scheme is  to provide hostel facilities to SC Boys and Girls studying in middle schools, 
higher secondary schools, colleges and Universities.  The Scheme provides for release of 
central assistance to State Governments on 50:50 basis for construction of Hostels for 
Boys and 100% for hostel for Girls belonging to Scheduled Castes.  The Union Territory 
Administrations receive 100% central assistance.  Further, one time grant of Rs. 2500/ - 
per student is also given for a cot, table and a chair.  The maintenance of hostel s, 
boarding and lodging of students, however, rest with the respective States/UTs.  The Non-
Governmental Organizations also get assistance under the scheme on the basis of 

48 
 
45:45:10 from Central Government, State Governments and NGO share respectively for 
extension of their existing hostels.  This support is provided through the State 
Government.  The Central Universities can receive financial assistance upto 90% under 
the scheme and the remaining 10% is required to be contributed by them.  Likewise, other 
universities can also receive central assistance upto 45% and the remaining amount has 
to be provided by their respective States (45%) and themselves (10%).

NATIONAL BACKWARD CLASSES FINANCE AND DEVELOPMENT 
CORPORATION  
 
5.1 The National Backward Classes Finance and Development Corporation 
(NBCFDC) was set up in the year 1992, as a company, „not for profit‟ under secti on 25 of 
the Companies Act 1956.  Out of the authorized share capital of Rs. 700/ - crore, the 
Government of India has released Rs. 491.35 crore till 2007 -08.  During 2008 -09, a sum 
of Rs. 36 crore was released raising paid -up capital of the Corporation to Rs. 527.35 
crore.  The Corporation provides additional channel of finance to backward classes for 
economically and financially viable schemes and projects for upgrading the technological 
and entrepreneurial skills of individuals or groups belonging to Back ward Classes.   
NBCFDC assists a wide range of income generating activities, which include agricultural 
and allied activities, artisan and traditional occupations, technical trades, small scale and 
tiny industry, transport services etc. Entrepreneurs with annual income less than double 
the poverty line are provided concessional finance. 
NBCFDC  implements various schemes through State Channelling Agencies 
(SCAs) for financial assistance as under : 
(i) Term Loan and Margin Money Loan: Under Term Loan Scheme,  loans are 
given by the Corporation upto 85% of the project cost, Balance 15% is contributed 
by SCAs and beneficiaries.  Under Margin Money Loan Scheme, loans upto 40% 
are  provided  by  the  Corporation  and  the  balance  60% is  contributed by 

58 
 
SCAs/beneficiaries and Banks/other Financial Institutions.  Maximum loan limit per 
beneficiary is Rs. 5 lakh only at interest of @6% p.a. 
(ii) Education Loan ‘New Aakanksha ’: For pursuing professional/technical 
education at graduate and higher levels.  Maximum loan  limit per student is Rs. 
1.25 lakh p.a. subject to maximum of Rs. 5.00 lakh or actual expenses for the 
entire course whichever is less.  Rate of interest is 4% p.a. 
(iii) Micro Finance: Loans are provided to Self Help Groups (SHGs) through SCAs.  
Maximum amount of loan under this scheme is upto Rs. 25,000/ - per beneficiary.  
Rate of interest is 5% p.a. 
(iv) Special Schemes for Women: 
a) New Swarnima:- 
The Scheme is implemented for inculcating the spirit of self-reliance among the 
women of Backward Classes liv ing below the poverty line.  Financial 
assistance to the extent of Rs. 50,000/ - per beneficiary is provided at 
concessional rate of interest of 4% per annum. 
b) Mahila Samridhi Yojana 
 
The Scheme is implemented to provide micro finance to women entrepreneurs 
belonging to target group.  The maximum loan limit per beneficiary is Rs. 
25000/- at concessional rate of interest of 4% per annum.

cross the below poverty line.  It becomes easier for the beneficiaries to avail the 
loans if the State Governments provide State Guarantee to these loans.  The 
Committee, h owever, find that a very discouraging and non -desirable trend has 
developed over a period of time  where many States are showing their reluctance to 
act as State Guarantor to NBCFDC loans. The Committee  have learnt  that   the 
States of Assam, Bihar, Manipur and Uttar Pradesh are not providi ng the state 
guarantee thereby depriving many prospective beneficiaries from availing NBCFDC 
loans.  The Committee also observe that some States are also charging guarantee 
fee (in some cases it is upto 2% charged by State Governments from State 
Channelising Agencies).  Whereas   thi s minimal charge is not contributing to the 
State treasuries in a substantial way, this provision is certainly acting as a deterrent 
in availing the NBCDFC loans by the OBCs. The Committee, therefore, recommend 
strongly that the Ministry should impress upon the States to act as State guarantor  
and also not to charge any guarantee fees from SCAs,  so that the poor OBC people 
do not get debarred from availing NBCFDC loans.

entrepreneurial skills are also provided to eligible members of the other Backward

Scheme has reduced from 2801 in 2007-08 to only 1319 during the year 2008 -09. On

been informed that at present the ceiling of annual family income of beneficiaries 
being very low, i.e., Rs. 55000, a large se ction of meritorious students of the

unrealistic considering the consumer price index. Therefore, the Committee desire

the income ceiling to Rs.2.25 so that the momentum of the scheme does not slow 
down and more number of beneficiaries are able to avail the benefits of the scheme.

a downward spiral during this period, yet  the process of employment generation 
was still going on in the various sectors of the economy.  While the Committee 
understand the limitations of the Ministry relating to the  ‘non -binding’ and 
‘voluntary’ nature of the scheme, yet concerted efforts should have been made to at 
least popularize the ‘concept’ among the private players through rigorous 
canvassing, widespread propaganda and publicity.  The Committee feel that leaving 
the subject at the mercy of the private sector has not worked.  Since the scheme 
has failed to evoke any interest among the private sector, the Committee 
recommend that  the performance of the scheme should be closely watched and 
intensive efforts should be made to p opularize the scheme by utilizing the entire 
amount earmarked for the purpose  during the remaining period of the  current year.  
The Committee are of the view that i f the scheme  still fails to attract the private 
sector, the Ministry should think of discont inuing the scheme in its present form 
and make efforts to bring in a legislation with mandatory provisions.   

75 
 
CHAPTER VII 
NEW SCHEME  
PRADHAN MANTRI  ADHARSH GRAM YOJANA (PMAGY) 
7.1 As per the information in the outcome budget of the Ministry a new scheme named 
Pradhan Mantri Adharsh Gram Yojana is being introduced during the year 2009-10 with an 
allocation of 100 crores for integrated development of villages having more than 40% SC 
population as model villages. When asked as to whether the Planning Commission has 
already approved the above scheme and has the Ministry already launched the above 
scheme, the Ministry in their written reply informed the Committee that  the Finance 
Minister, in his Budget Speech, 2009-10, delivered on 6.7.2009, announced launching of a 
new scheme, namely “Pradhan Mantri Adarsh Gram Yojana”, on pilot basis, to cover 1000 
villages with more than 50% SC population. The relevant para of the speech reads as 
under :- 
“Pradhan Mantri Adarsh Gram Yojana (PMAGY) 
  
46 (v) There are about 44,000 villages in which the population of Scheduled castes 
is above 50 percent. A new scheme called  Pradhan Mantri Adarsh Gram Yojana  
(PMAGY) is being launched this year on a pilot basis, for the integrated development of 
1000 such villages. I propose an allocation of Rs. 100 crore for this scheme. Each 
village would be able to avail gap funding of Rs. 10 lakh over and above the allocations 
under Rural Development and Poverty Allevi ation Schemes. On successful 
implementation of the pilot phase, the Yojana would be extended in coming years.” 
 
7.2 In pursuance of the above announcement, a Concept Note for the scheme was sent 
by the Ministry to the Planning Commission on 18.8.2009 for its “in principle” approval. The 
Commission, vide its O.M. dated 26.8.09, has given its “in principle” approval. Detailed 
proposal of the scheme will now be considered by the Expenditure Finance Committee. 

76 
 
Thereafter, approval by the competent authority wil l be obtained, and the scheme will be 
formally launched. 
7.3  About the salient features, coverage and objectives of the proposed scheme, the 
Ministry further informed the Committee as under :- 
 In the pilot phase the scheme will cover 1,000 selected villa ges with >50% SC 
population.  Main objective of the scheme is to ensure integrated development of the 
selected 1000 villages with more than 50% SC population into “model villages” so that, 
inter -alia, 
(i) They have all requisite physical and social infrastructure for their socio -
economic development. 
(ii) Disparity between SC and non -SC population in terms of common socio -
economic indicators (e.g. literacy rate, completion rate of elementary 
education, IMR/MMR, ownership of productive assets,  etc.) is eliminated, 
the indicators are raised to at least the level of the  national average, and : 
(a) All their BPL families, especially those belonging to SCs, have food 
and livelihood, security, and are enabled to cross the poverty line and 
earn an adequate livelihood; 
(b) All children complete at least eight years of education; and  
(c) Incidence of malnutrition, especially among children and women, is 
eliminated. 
(iii) Untouchability, discrimination, segregation, and atrocities against SCs are 
eliminated, as are other social e vils like discrimination against girls/women, 

77 
 
alcoholism and substance ( drugs) abuse, etc., and all sections of society  
are able to live with dignity and equality, and in harmony  with others. 
  
7.4 When asked about the action plan of the Ministry for pr oper implementation of the 
above scheme, the Committee were further informed that the integrated development of 
villages with SC concentration will be achieved primarily through  convergent 
implementation of existing Central and State schemes.  A component  of gap-filling fund, at 
an average rate of Rs. 10 lakh per village, will be used for meeting specifically identified 
developmental requirements of selected villages which cannot be met under the existing 
schemes of the Central and State Governments. The d evelopment plans will be need -
based. In order to ensure this, the preparation and appraisal/ approval of village level 
plans will be decentralized.  Mechanism for supervision and monitoring will be put in place 
at the District, State and Central levels. 
 
7.5 The Committee were also informed that the details of the scheme, including 
modalities of its implementation and detailed guidelines for implementing agencies are 
being worked out. All the concerned Ministries, especially those implementing schemes 
which are directly relevant for SC development, are being consulted while finalizing details 
of the scheme.  
 
7.6 The Committee have been  informed that in pursuance of the Finance 
Minister’s Budget announcement, the Ministry are planning to launch the Pradhan 
Mantri Aadarsh Gram Yojana (PMAGY) on pilot basis to cover 1000 villages with 
more than 50% SC population and an allocation of Rs. 100 crore has been 
earmarked for the scheme during the year 2009 -10.  The Committee are happy to 

78 
 
note that f or the first time a serious thought has been given for  area oriented 
integrated development of villages with SC concentration through convergent 
implementation of  existing Central and State schemes. While the Committee 
appreciate the initiative taken by the Ministry, the actual impact of the scheme in 
achieving integrated development of area having SC people concentration will be 
seen only after it is actually implemented. The Committee recommend that while 
every effort should be made to finalise the intricate details of t he scheme at the 
earliest and implement it in an efficient manner, a thorough homework should be 
done before the launch of the scheme taking into consideration the on g round 
conditions of the target villages.  The Committee hope that efforts would be made to 
utilize the entire amount judiciously  during the current financial year  and no scope 
would be left to the Planning Commission for  the reversal of the amount allocated 
for the purpose during the next financial year.  The Committee would like to be 
apprised of the steps taken in this direction by the Ministry.

STATEMENT OF OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS
